subtopic: VIET NAM-ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMONWEALTH PEACE MISSION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: VIET NAM-ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMONWEALTH PEACE MISSION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Acting Prime Minister. In view of the announcement from London that a Commonwealth peace mission will seek to end the war in Viet Nam, could the Acting Prime Minister, in his usual terse and informative manner, give the House the benefit of information he undoubtedly has received from London in this regard? Could he also state what is Canada's position with regard to the touring peace mission; and why was the decision made that the Prime Minister of Canada would not be one of the Commonwealth leaders represented on this mission, in view of Canada's great interest in securing stability and peace in the international sphere?

subtopic: VIET NAM-ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMONWEALTH PEACE MISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the day before yesterday I told the right hon. Leader of the Opposition that the Government had received a communication from the British Government and that we were aware of a proposal which was going to be made the following day by the British Prime Minister. That proposal was made yesterday and was accepted by the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference. It provides for the Prime Ministers of the countries designated, under the chairmanship of the British Prime Minister, to proceed first to the United Nations Secretary General, then to other interested countries, the United States, South and North Viet Nam, the Chinese People's Republic, and the Soviet Union, with a view to impressing on all governments concerned the desirability of entering into discussions that might bring about an end to hostilities in Viet Nam.
The Prime Minister of Canada was interested and active in suggestions with regard to this proposal. His well known participation in endeavours to provide for conditions of peace in the world, which brought him the Nobel peace prize, was undoubtedly considered when it was proposed that he be a member of this group. The Prime Minister of Canada, rightly in my judgment, took the position that, as it was desirable to have a balanced representation on this delegation of Prime Ministers of the Commonwealth it would be better if this balance were preserved. It is not that the Prime Minister did not want to participate; it is because he thought if the move were to be successful the mission must represent as many sections of the Commonwealth as was possible. This view was finally concurred in by other members of the conference.
I am sure I express the views of this Parliament, Mr. Speaker, when I say that we sincerely hope all governments concerned will receive this delegation, which represents the most important single grouping of nations in the world. The delegation will undoubtedly express, what I think most people would want them to express, namely that the problem of Viet Nam can be resolved better by conciliation and discussion than by the use of force.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: VIET NAM-ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMONWEALTH PEACE MISSION
speechtext: A supplementary question. The Acting Prime Minister said that the reason for the Canadian Prime Minister not being included in this peace mission was to preserve a balance. I wonder whether he could explain to us, because of the doubts I have on this aspect, what he means by "balance"?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: VIET NAM-ESTABLISHMENT OF COMMONWEALTH PEACE MISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope my hon. friend will not seek to give the impression-I know he would not wish to because he wants this mission to succeed, as we all do-that the position taken by the Prime Minister is open to question. The Prime Minister of Britain represents the western group of the Commonwealth in this delegation. If the Prime Minister of Canada were also to be included in this delegation of five, this would mean there would be representation from two western countries which are members of NATO. I think the position taken by the Prime Minister of Canada was not only proper but wise.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare regarding a Canadian Press dispatch from Regina which says that the Saskatchewan health department will appeal a magistrate's ruling that all Indians should receive free hospital and medical care from the Federal Government. The dispatch goes on to say that Health Minister D. G. Stewart, in a press release yesterday, said that the appeal decision was made after consultation with Federal Government officials, and that these officials were of the opinion that the ramifications of the judgment are such that the case should be appealed.
I want to ask the Minister whether this statement is correct and, if it is, why the Canadian Government is endeavouring to evade its responsibilities in supplying health services to the Indians of this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. Judy V. LaMarsh (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: COURT DECISION RESPECTING PROVISION OF MEDICAL CARE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement is quite correct. The Minister of Health and the Attorney General of Saskatchewan have notified us of the result of the case, and consultation has been had with the Immigration Branch and the Department of Justice. The appeal will be taken because of the very far-reaching implications of the decision.
My hon. friend will recall that when he was Premier of the Province which brought in medicare legislation he did not include Indians, who thus became a different class of citizen. It is considered for the native people of the country extraordinarily important that this treaty, which contains health provisions similar to those of other treaties, be construed by a court higher than a magistrate's court so the matter may be settled once and for all.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I believe the only questions remaining unanswered are those raised by the hon. Member for Edmonton West and the hon. Member for Port Arthur. I must say that the questions they did raise appear to me to be of considerable substance. Perhaps I might deal with a question raised by the hon. Member for Port Arthur. As reported at page 2589 of Hansard the hon. Member asked this question:
-under the guise of some kind of culture some Canadian magazine in existence, and it might even be a defunct property like Liberty which probably has a copyright and is entitled to the name, to merge with some United States publications so that we would get a situation where we have in effect a replica of the Time and Reader's Digest situation.
I must concede at once that this appeared to me to be a very valid question, and I did not see the solution in the Customs Tariff Act. However, the officials have directed my attention to the Income Tax Act and I believe the answer can be found there. In other words, the hon. Member for Port Arthur was inquiring whether it would be possible for a large foreign publishing organization to make use of the title of a defunct Canadian periodical and so have in Canada a periodical which would draw its editorial matter from different periodicals in the United States or elsewhere. I should like to point out that under the income tax resolution such a publication, even though printed in Canada, would not qualify as Canadian by virtue of section 5(a)(ii)(F). Perhaps, Mr. Chairman, I may refer to that section, which defines what is meant by "Canadian issue":
but does not include an issue of a periodical
(E) that is produced or published under a licence granted by a person who produces or publishes issues of a periodical that are printed, edited or published outside Canada-
Then going to subparagraph (F):
the contents of which, excluding advertisements, are substantially the same as the contents of an issue of a periodical, or the contents of one or more issues of one or more periodicals, that was or were printed, edited or published outside Canada;
I believe that covers the very fundamental point raised by the hon. Member for Port Arthur. He went on to raise a further question. The hon. Member was concerned about the effect of this legislation on the entry into Canada of publications such as Saturday Evening Post, New Republic, Harper's and other prominent publications which circulate

nationally both in the United States and in Canada.
May I say, Mr. Chairman, that it does not seem to me, with respect, that the proposed tariff item will have much effect on the circulation of this type of publication in Canada. None of these periodicals, so far as I am informed, at present publishes split runs or regional editions, and to this extent they will not be affected by the provisions of item 1221 (1). These periodicals, of course, like all foreign periodicals will be required to meet the test of item 1221 (2). In other words they will have to ensure that not more than 5 per cent of the advertising space in any issue consists of space used for advertisements indicating specific sources of availability in Canada. I doubt very much whether this will prove to be a very onerous requirement for these publications, and I believe that most of the foreign periodicals which circulate in Canada are already meeting these requirements.
The hon. Member went on to raise a third question about the scope of the exemptions in the proposed tariff item as they relate to such publications as coin catalogues. I acknowledge that this is a matter that would have to be examined very carefully by the customs officials in each individual case to see whether the publication in question was a genuine catalogue or simply a trade magazine. This is going to require the exercise of judgment, but I think so far as these catalogues are concerned the officials have been on the whole rather generous in their interpretations.
The fourth point raised by the hon. Member for Port Arthur dealt with special issues of publications devoted to Canada. The question here is whether they are special editions for circulation in Canada, in which case they would be prohibited under item 1221 (1) if they contained any advertisement primarily directed to a market in Canada. So that while it may be a special edition devoted to Canada, the test is whether the advertising is primarily directed to a market in Canada. For instance, you could have a special issue devoted to Canada but directed to a market in the United States. You might have a travel magazine publishing a special issue to bring tourists into Canada, so the advertising would be directed to people in the United States although there would be a special issue devoted to Canada.
I should also point out that if a travel magazine published a special issue devoted to news and articles about Canada, and the

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That is right; my hon. friend interjects correctly. I also understand that the publishing firms have been in close contact with officials of the Department. They are people who, of course, will be very directly concerned with this legislation. They are aware of all its implications, and when it does come into effect I think they will be in the position to make the necessary adjustments to meet the requirements of the amendment.

I doubt whether there is anyone more informed as to the effect of this legislation than the hon. Member. The point is that there has been a significant amount of magazine advertising directed to Canadians which has originated from companies situated outside of Canada. This legislation is aimed at containing that practice. I think it is recognized that this proposal is fairly well on all fours with the recommendation of the Royal Commission, with one slight exception with regard to the 5 per cent referred to in item 1221(2). So these magazines will be prohibited, as the item says.
There are two parts to item 1221. The first part says there will be a prohibition if it is an issue of a special edition, including a split run or a regional edition, that contains an advertisement that is primarily directed to a market in Canada and that does not appear in identical form in all editions of that issue of that periodical that were distributed in the country of origin. The second exception deals with the regular, ordinary issue, where it is found that more than 5 per cent of the advertising space consists of advertisements that indicate specific sources of availability in Canada, or specific terms or conditions relating to the sale or provision in Canada of any goods or services, except where the indication of such sources of availability or such terms and conditions is primarily directed to persons outside Canada.
I think that last exception covers the point raised regarding travel magazines. They would be directed to a market primarily outside of Canada. Although there could be a split edition relating to Canada, it might still be a regular edition.
On the question of date, the hon. Member asked about the effect of item 1221 (1), which refers to an issue dated after September 30, 1965. The only explanation I can offer-and this is subject to correction-is that it seems to me that if it came into effect on January 1, 1966, then if any one of the four preceding issues of a monthly publication violated the exemption clause, it would be prohibited. I think that is the proper explanation, although as I say it is subject to correction. I see the hon. Member is nodding his head, so it appears to be a reasonable explanation.

Just one further point. With regard to the regulations which will be prescribed by the Governor in Council, I realize that the normal procedure would likely be that they would be published in the Canada Gazette. However, in view of the fact that

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this subject was last discussed about a month ago, and at that time I said it seemed to me strange that the Government was proposing to set up a parliamentary committee to study the Canadian penitentiary system at the same time that a committee of experts headed by Mr. Justice Ouimet is studying the whole question of correction. It seems to me completely irresponsible on the part of the Government to be planning a major program of building penitentiaries to house people convicted of crimes before it has established just what the whole correctional program is to be.
I am not alone in this feeling, Mr. Speaker. If one reads the speeches which have been made by people who work in this field, and reads the articles which have appeared not only in technical journals but in newspapers and magazines across Canada, he will come to the same conclusion.
It is not often that I find myself in agreement with the Financial Post, but as long ago as August, 1963 that paper carried an article in relation to the whole question of Canadian prisons. That article pointed out several very interesting things. First of all, it stated that the Canadian prison population rose from 22,747 in 1962 to 23,512 in 1963. In the same period it pointed out that Britain's prison population dropped from 31,700 to 29,000. In view of the fact that Britain has a population approximately three times as large as the population of Canada, it is obvious that their approach is much more successful than the approach taken by Canada in this regard.
This article, as carried by the Winnipeg Free Press of November 14, 1964 stated: Physical conditions in some of our jails (and penitentiaries) are notoriously disgraceful. Overcrowding and poor discipline lead to riot. In Canada the percentage of released prisoners who 
return to crime and are again locked up is exceptionally high.
It further states:
We have no accepted official philosophy. We do not know whether we are merely trying to deter crime and protect society by isolating lawbreakers or whether our objective, in accordance with modern thought, is rehabilitation.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
In November of 1964 a series of articles appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press dealing with the problem of correction and penal reform, written by Mrs. Ellen Simmons, who has given a great deal of study to the question. I want to quote a couple of paragraphs from one article which appeared on November 16, 1964. She said:
What is needed first therefore-before any innovations in penal reform can hope for measurable, lasting success-is a clear, unflinchingly openeyed and open-minded look at the system, if indeed it may be called a system, in use in Canada today. Specific reforms that have been proposed are meaningful only in the total context of a coherent purposeful philosophy for the treatment of lawbreakers.
She points out some examples of what is wrong and the differences between provinces. I continue quoting:
For example, the use of probation is almost unknown in Prince Edward Island. It is seldom used in Quebec. But in Ontario probation is used in some 21 per cent of cases involving offences against property. Similarly, suspended sentences are used most sparingly in British Columbia, while in Manitoba they are used with a comparatively free hand.
I give these illustrations because it seems to me it is completely wrong for the Government to propose that a parliamentary committee look at the building program when that program has already been decided upon by the Government. When I spoke on this matter over a month ago I mentioned that a judge familiar with the Government's program in Ontario had made a speech in which he said that well over $100 million would be spent for new prisons by the Canadian Government in the next 10 years. I am not opposed to new buildings or the rebuilding of our institutions. Most of them date back many years. Most of them are a disgrace to any civilized country. But surely before going ahead with a program we ought to know what we are doing, what the requirements are and what kind of people are going to be put in the institutions we intend to build.
There is no better illustration of the fact that we do not know these things and have not arrived at any conclusions than the special detention units which are planned
June 18. 1965
and in fact are already being built. I understand that the one in Quebec is going ahead at a great rate. It is not my intention to read into the record again the whole of the telegram sent to the Minister of Justice by the Canadian Corrections Association, but as it is more than a month since I spoke on the matter I should like to read one paragraph:
These special detention units are completely unacceptable to the Canadian Corrections Association on the basis of scientific evidence related to the effects of psychological and physical isolation. Among other things we fear the deterioration of inmates who are confined in cells without windows.
I had an opportunity to discuss this matter with a psychiatrist who works in Canadian prisons. I am not going to mention his name because he told me that he intended to discuss the matter directly with the Minister of Justice, whom he knows. However, I think I can quote him almost exactly. He said it was his intention to say to the Minister of Justice that on the basis of his experience in working with prisoners who are emotionally and mentally disturbed, it was his view that if a person was not psychotic before entering one of these institutions which the Government is proposing to build he would almost certainly be psychotic by the time he got out. Despite the unanimous advice of experts in the field, the Government and the Minister stubbornly insist on going ahead with the building program. It seems to me that to ask a parliamentary committee to look into these matters when the Government has already indicated to the people interested that they intend to go ahead is really ridiculous and a waste of time.
I want to make a further point with regard to the prison building program. It seems to me and to other people that if we send people to prison we ought to know why we are sending them there. It seems to me that before sending people to prison we should ask ourselves whether it is best for them to be sent to prison or would it be better to try something else. Ontario and British Columbia have been very successful with their systems of probation. People convicted of crimes are placed under the supervision of probation officers rather than being sent to prison.
Rather than a costly program of building institutions for the confinement of people, it seems to me that we should be expanding our probation system. I know that because of divided jurisdiction the matter of probation comes under the provinces, but I can see no reason why the Federal Government should not co-operate financially in a vast expansion 22620-166J
Joint Committee on Penitentiaries of the probation system so the prison population of Canada would go down instead of going up from year to year. I am satisfied, and the experts are satisfied, that the results then would be much better than they have been.
The Minister has appointed a committee to look at the whole question of corrections, and in the resolution now before us he is proposing to appoint a parliamentary committee to look at our prison institutions. If there is one thing we have done in the field of corrections in this country, it has been to appoint royal commissions and committees of experts to look at the problem. But once they have made their reports, which have been excellent, we have promptly forgotten them; they have been filed away to gather dust.
When the Parliamentary Secretary spoke on this subject he referred to the Archambault report. I do not know why he did so when he could have referred to the more recent Fauteux report. I do not want to go into detail with regard to the Fauteux report, but I should like to quote one recommendation which is found on page 87. The Commission recommended as follows:
Some means should be found whereby the courts, at all levels, may be made more conscious that the true purpose of punishment is the correction of the offender and not mere retribution by society.
That was true when the Fauteux report was published almost 10 years ago, and it is true today. Professor Angus made a speech in Alberta recently in which he was critical of the kind of people who are appointed as judges.

The hon. Member for Edmonton West says he had holes in his head. I happen to agree with Professor Angus. The Minister of Justice was also quite critical of this professor. I want to put on record some of the sentences that have been pronounced in recent days from one end of Canada to the other. I quote from the Globe and Mail of May 12, 1965. The article is rather short and is headed "Quebec Convict Hangs Himself with His Belt". As the story is not long I will put the whole thing on the record. The article reads as follows:
Police said Saturday that Jean-Guy Genereux, 28, a prisoner at nearby St. Vincent de Paul Penitentiary, hanged himself with his belt Friday night. Details were sketchy but police said Genereux, serving a 13 year term for the armed robbery of a suburban Verdun hardware store, was found dead in his cell around 10.30 p.m.
Genereux was sentenced by Sessions Judge Jacques Trahan Wednesday. He admitted robbing the

store February 11. He was captured minutes alter the robbery and police recovered $10.77 taken from the store and another $7 from a post office on the premises. Before sentencing Genereux, Judge Trahan said: "Making long speeches to people like you is a waste of time and the only way to deal with animals like you is to lock you up for a considerable length of time."
[DOT] (12:20 p.m.)
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether Judge Trahan has ever heard of the Fauteux Commission or its recommendations. What kind of impartial, objective attitude is this for a judge to take? Here was a man who appeared in court before Judge Trahan the day after he was apprehended for the tremendous crime of robbery which netted him some $17. He appeared without counsel. I challenge anybody in this House to question my statement that had he had counsel, in any part of Canada, no judge or magistrate would have spoken the way Judge Trahan spoke. What kind of judge is it, what kind of human is it who would speak in such terms of a person who is in trouble? He called this person an animal. Mr. Speaker, I think Judge Trahan should be in prison for that kind of speech. A person with this approach is a disgrace to Canadian courts. When the Minister of Justice and the Member for Edmonton West defend that kind of judge, I do not believe they realize the situation we are facing.
Well, Mr. Speaker, Judge Trahan is not alone. I have before me a photostatic copy of the Montreal Gazette for September 21, 1963 in which there are two stories side by side. One story has this headline: "Crown Witness in $500,000 Theft Gets One Day, Plus Time in Jail". I quote from the article:
Jacques Lajoie, the 38 year old star witness for the crown in a $500,000 bank vault burglary case of April, 1962, pleaded guilty yesterday to being a participant in the spectacular robbery and had a one day prison term tacked on to the 21 months he has been in jail.
It is interesting to note, incidentally, that he appeared before Mr. Justice Roger Ouimet, who is on the committee which has been appointed by the Minister to look into the whole question of corrections. Right below this article there is another story which carries the headline: "$1.65 Loot-10 years". I quote from the article:
Violent and audacious crimes which today have become common place in Montreal will not be stopped by goodwill and kindness any more effectively than would cancer in the human body.
Then I quote from what Judge Claude Wagner said:
[Mr. Orlikow.l
"The courts must act as surgeons," declared Sessions Judge Claude Wagner yesterday afternoon in a judgment which found Philip Moffat, Tasse St., guilty of an armed robbery of a pair of gloves worth $1.65 from a Verdun store.
Judge Wagner sentenced Moffat to ten years in penitentiary.
Again, I am sure Mr. Philip Moffat had no counsel, so that on very short notice he was tried and sentenced to ten years. Anyone who is involved in something like Windfall or something like Texas Sulphur, where the stakes are much greater than $1.65 and run into the hundreds of thousands of dollars, can afford eminent counsel who can spin out the time before justice catches up with him. He can get off with a reprimand or a pat on the wrist, it seems to me. The hon. Member for Timiskaming reminds me that he may even keep his judgeship, but that is a subject we can discuss on another occasion.
It seems to me we have a great deal of work to do, and not just the appointment of a committee. I do not want to be accused of being anti-Quebec because the two illustrations I used were from the Province of Quebec. I should like to put on record a few paragraphs from a case in my own city, my own Province, concerning a husband and wife who happened to live in the constituency of my hon. friend the Member for Winnipeg North Centre, and who happened to be Indians. They were charged with a breach of the Child Welfare Act. They appeared before Magistrate Isaac Rice, Q.C. several months ago. Again, they appeared without counsel. I feel this is one of the most disgraceful cases I have ever read, and I should like to read into the record part of the testimony. I quote:
Magistrate: Hold old are you?
A. Thirty-four.
Magistrate: Thirty-four, and you have already brought in 12 children into the world. She is
good for another 15 at the rate she is going. You are young enough to produce a lot more-
Then the Crown Prosecutor, Mr. Montgomery, said:
Your Worship, I can make a respectful submission as to how there might be five less children.
The magistrate asked how, and Mr. Montgomery answered:
Under the particular statute, the legislature has provided for a term of imprisonment of up to five years.
What a travesty of justice. Now, is there a single member of this House who can say that if the people appearing before the magistrate had not been Indians living in a slum area of Winnipeg but had been white Anglo-Saxon Protestants living in the constituency
June 18. 1965

of the hon. Member for Winnipeg South, the magistrate would have spoken so irresponsibly?

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: You mean the Member appeared before the magistrate?

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
No, I said if it had been one of her constituents or a constituent of any Member or former Member of Parliament. What I am trying to say is that in this country, unfortunately, we have one law for the well to do, the people who have money and can be represented by counsel, and another, entirely different and much harsher law for people who do not have the money to obtain counsel who will help to defend them and who will also assure that the kind of sentence they get will be much less.
These are things, Mr. Speaker, which people expert in the field have been discussing for a long period of time. These are the things which this Government seems to be ignoring. We have appointed another committee, headed by Mr. Justice Ouimet and composed of some excellent members. I know some of the members and they will not be the kind of rubber-stamp committee which this Government so often wants. I am hopeful, in fact I am certain, they are going to make some excellent recommendations. It seems to me that unless we do a great deal more about the recommendations they are likely to make than past Parliaments have done about the Archambault report and the Fauteux report, Canada will continue to be among the last half dozen of the western industrialized countries in so far as their records in the field of corrections are concerned.
I am not going to oppose the setting up of this committee, because the Government has indicated clearly it intends to proceed. I hope the work of this committee will not be done in a vacuum; that the Government will realize that they cannot simply build prisons without at the same time looking at the whole field of correction, the whole field of probation, sentencing and bail. My colleague the hon. Member for Danforth raised the serious question of bail the other day and received a miserable, disgraceful answer from the Parliamentary Secretary, one of the worst I have heard since I have been in the House. If that is an indication of the seriousness with which the Department regards legitimate questions about the system of corrections in this country, then we are indeed in for some difficult periods. They will be difficult in this House because I can tell the Parliamentary

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries Secretary that if he continues that line in committee-I presume he will be a member- we will have many long hours of sitting. The Members on this side of the House are not going to take the nonsensical kind of argument he produced the other night.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, the committee will work in co-operation with the special committee which the Minister of Justice has appointed. I hope we will get on with the work, and that it will not be years before we can begin the major task of reorganizing the correctional system of this country so the purpose may become rehabilitation rather than punishment, as has been the case for the last 100 years.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I agree with very much of what has been said by the previous speaker. For years we have talked about the shocking state of our penal institutions in Canada. Reports of various commissions and committees have been debated in the House of Commons. The previous speaker mentioned the Archambault report, the report of the Fauteux commission and reports of committees such as the present Government is now instigating. The recommendations contained in all these reports have been abundantly clear. I will refer to them later, though I make special reference in passing to one of the best commission reports ever published in the Dominion of Canada; that is the Archambault report. I think all hon. Members will agree that the subject we are discussing today can be considered in a bipartisan sense.
Much has been done in this field of penal reform in the past few years, but it is still too little. I know that in 1957 the party which I support did its best. There were many accomplishments to our credit in such fields as the ticket of leave and parole system, getting a realistic building program under way, and properly staffing our penal institutions. While I would be the first to admit that we have only made a beginning and, in a sense, a poor beginning, and that far too little has been accomplished, a start has certainly been made in the field of penal reform.
Along with Members opposite I recognize the difficulties which are involved. Sometimes it is very hard in this day and age to rally public opinion behind modern concepts of penology. I believe all governments have encountered this difficulty, but that is no excuse for failure to bring up this subject
June 18, 1965

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries time and time again on the floor of the House of Commons so that real advances can be made.
I think it is correct to say that in comparison with other countries we in Canada have an unbelievable number of inmates in our prisons; and not only in prisons but in prisons where the conditions are appalling. I will not belabour the House with statistics, but this seems abundantly clear from the figures which are available. It seems to me incredible that in relation to our population we should have such a large prison population both federal and provincial. For one reason or another we have an astonishingly high prison population in Canada compared with other countries in the western world.
We need to build many new penal institutions based on modern concepts. A beginning was made when we were in power, and the present Government is continuing this program and advancing new programs. But not enough has been done. The casual offender must be separated from the hardened criminal. This is a recommendation which has been made for years and years, but it is one which in the truest sense has not been carried out. In the whole field of penology we lack scores of probation and parole officers. Drug addiction and alcoholism have become major problems. We lack treatment centres for those who suffer from both these types of addiction. Many offenders in these categories should be treated immediately in centres where attention is paid to the modern science of psychiatry instead of being sent as they are now to old fashioned prisons. But what are we doing? Recommendations by one commission after another are listened to respectfully, but somehow or other we continue to send these people to old fashioned prisons after offences have been committed.
The consequences are abundantly clear. These people return to society and immediately repeat the same or similar crimes. We lack modern treatment centres, despite the need to send many people to such centres rather than to prison or other institutions built and staffed on archaic lines. Today these people are invariably sent to prisons, at high cost to the Government and at high cost to individual dignity. They are not cured and the public is not protected. Men or women who could be rehabilitated are not rehabilitated. An offender is released from prison and returns to society to commit the same or similar crimes.
I intend to quote some statistics. What are these statistics in Canada today? In 1964

some 74.2 per cent of those in federal penitentiaries had previously been committed to correctional institutions either federal or provincial. Need I say any more about the success of our system, a system of which no Member of this House of Commons should be proud? I do not say this in a party sense. I am sure Members in all corners of this House wish to co-operate in bettering the present system. That is why, I hope, we are setting up the new committee.
In the case of juvenile offenders there is a woeful lack of social welfare workers, judges, probation officers and parole officers. Young offenders, in addition to being segre-grated from older and more hardened criminals, must be able to continue their education while in institutions. Upon their release they must be able to re-enter society with every chance of obtaining employment. This means continuing vocational or academic training within the institution. I am glad that some advances have been made in this regard, but these advances have been minimal both when we were in power and under the administration of members opposite.
What is needed is action, and action now, as the hon. Member who spoke previously said so well. I realize it is difficult in a largely materialistic society to get public opinion behind such a program, but it is my hope the Government will realize the real need for action, and action now, rather than wait for the findings contained in yet another report. [DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
Before I go further I want to discuss something which I feel should be placed on the record immediately. Both inside and outside this House of Commons we often get into conversations relating to various aspects of penology; whether it should be rehabilitative or punitive, and that sort of tiling. But I think when we consider the success of our system we should have a more objective test. We should ask ourselves what are we doing to protect society; what are we doing to rehabilitate and upgrade, if you will, the prisoner himself; what are we doing to reduce the level of recidivism in this country? If we apply these standards to measure the success of our whole system of penology in Canada we find that we are doing a very poor job.
I think every Member of the Canadian House of Commons should be aware of the following statistics. What percentage of those committed to penal institutions in Canada had a previous commitment to a penitentiary
June 18>
1965

only, namely an institution under federal jurisdiction? In 1961 the figure was 42 per cent; in 1962, 41.3 per cent; in 1963, 41.1 per cent; in 1964, 41.6 per cent. But the following statistics are even more astounding, Sir. What percentage of those committed had previous commitments to any correctional institution, be it federal or provincial? These, Sir, are most appalling statistics. In 1961, 72.2 per cent; in 1962, 76.7 per cent; in 1963, 76.8 per cent; and in 1964, 77.2 per cent.
What does this mean in hard facts? It means that at this moment, on June 18, 1965, in the case of people released from our institutions, be they federal or provincial there is almost an 80 per cent chance that they will go out into society and commit the same or similar crimes. These figures should be really digested by all Members of the House and by the Canadian public. Surely they show that in this area the main things that are good in modern penology are not being done in Canada. In the light of these statistics we are not protecting the public, our women and children and the population in general. Certainly in the light of these statistics we are not rehabilitating offenders, and we are not bringing down the percentage of recidivism in our prison population.
I understand, and support in a sense, the setting up of a committee such as we are discussing today. But surely it will be a committee that will discuss some modem penology concepts; because the statistics and what I have already said show that we in Canada are decades behind in the field of social reform. They show that we have not even begun to move forward in embracing and implementing the major, modern concepts of penology. I simply want to say, Sir, that I fully realize that in a field such as penology, in view of the advances that have been made in the last two decades in psychiatric research and treatment, we are faced with the application of many new and modern concepts, and certainly we should apply them.
Perhaps the Archambault report as such did not make too much reference to these modern concepts which have come to light in the last two decades. But I want to illustrate right now why many people in Canada become cynical about royal commissions, why many people in Canada become cynical about Parliament setting up committees, why many people in Canada become cynical about meeting after meeting,
Joint Committee on Penitentiaries commission after commission, when what is needed is action.
Surely we haven't the nerve to go out and tell the people that a lot is going to be done by a parliamentary committee when the major recommendations of a 1938 royal commission have not even been touched upon or discussed sensibly in this House of Commons.
The hon. Member who just spoke rightfully talked about a more modem inquiry into our penal system, namely the Fauteux Commission. We are now talking in glowing terms about what this parliamentary committee is going to do, but let me take the time of the House for a few moments to discuss some of the major recommendations of the Archambault report. Let us ask ourselves whether they have been truly implemented, and whether we really need a parliamentary committee to tell us what needs to be done today, not tomorrow, in the field of modern penal reform.
This is why the Canadian people become cynical. When a government should act, when a government should move forward almost without debate in the House of Commons, they set up a parliamentary committee or a royal commission. In this case it is even more serious, because anybody who has read the Archambault report would recognize and understand that it is one of the greatest, most important and best drafted royal commission reports in the whole history of this nation.
I believe that a great deal of importance should be attached to a parliamentary committee if it is going to act. But let us briefly search our consciences and look over some of the basic recommendations of the Archambault Royal Commission report. Then let us ask ourselves honestly whether these recommendations have been carried out. Let us ask ourselves, do we need another parliamentary committee in order to tell us what needs to be done?
I will enter a caveat here, Sir, and say there are some detailed matters which this committee should consider; there are some modem concepts that the committee should deal with. I refer to concepts which have come to light since the Archambault report and its recommendations were drafted. But in the next few minutes I am going to talk about the necessity to act today, not tomorrow, on some of the major recommendations of this report. Surely, Sir, when I read some of the recommendations drafted in the year 1938 by this eminent gentleman and his assistants on that Royal Com-
June 18, 1965

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries mission it will be abundantly clear why so many Canadians become cynical about royal commissions and parliamentary committees.
What did the Commissioner say, Sir, about the general approach to penology as such? He said in his recommendations that our whole concept should be based on the protection of society. Surely I have given statistics which show that we are not protecting society very well under our present penal system. He talked about the safe custody of inmates. I have no statistics in this connection, Sir. I am sure we have as many or as few escapes as other countries. Then the commissioner spoke about strict but humane discipline. I do not know how we compare with other countries in this regard. Then he dealt with the reform and rehabilitation of prisoners. I have already said that we have done a woeful job in this regard.
[DOT] (12:50 p.m.)
What do these recommendations go on to say regarding the classification of prisoners? With the modern buildings to house inmates being built at the present time under the direction of the Department of Justice, advances are going to be made in this direction. But surely not enough advances are being made; we are moving too slowly. I think primarily of St. Vincent de Paul and Kingston penitentiaries. If more Canadians were made to visit these institutions the Minister and his assistants would surely have a much easier time in geting public opinion behind the important work which I know the Government is trying to do in this regard.
How far have we gone in the last 30 years in carrying out these recommendations, and what will a further committee of this House be able to tell us about classification of prisoners? The Archambault commission reported that a complete revision of classification of prisoners should be made, with provision for a thorough medical and psychiatric examination. Their next recommendation is:
The necessary legislation should be enacted to provide for sentencing habitual offenders to preventive detention in a separate institution to be provided for that purpose.
Thirty years after this recommendation was made we are barely beginning to scratch the surface, and now all we are doing is setting up another parliamentary committee. They further recommended:
All incorrigible and intractable prisoners in the penitentiaries should be segregated in one institution.
Separate institutions, based on the principles of the English Borstal system, should be established

to permit of special treatment being given to young offenders between sixteen and twenty-one years of age.
We have made a beginning here, but only a very small beginning. The recommendation continues:
There should also be a classification centre and three grades in each unit, each grade to be separately located and not contiguous to another. Two units should be established at once, one in the
Province of Ontario, and one in the province of Quebec-
The next recommendation is:
All insane prisoners should be entirely removed from the prison population and treated in hospitals for the insane.
This bears on my recommendation that something be done to fill the great need today for psychiatric units, not only for the insane but also for drug addicts and alcoholics, instead of just throwing them into prison and hoping that after five or six years they will be able to emerge into public life without having had any treatment. Then it is recommended that:
The mentally deficient should be segregated in the ordinary institutions under the direction of a trained psychiatrist.
Intractable and recidivist drug addicts should be removed on the order of the prison commission to the prison for habitual offenders.
A scheme of classification should be established in each prison, having regard to the previous record, social habits, physical condition, educational attainments, aptitudes, and suitable training for future employment, of individual prisoners.
A grades and merit system for reformable prisoners, modelled on the system in use in England, should be established.
Let us ask ourselves, as we pause for a moment after looking at these recommendations, how far have we gone in even scratching the surface and making headway in this regard?
What does the Archambault Commission have to say about education? Since this report was published I think all hon. Members will admit that we have made some progress in this field, but it is such little progress that we should all be ashamed of it. It was recommended that:
A complete reorganization of the educational system should be made in accordance with the recommendations contained in chapter VIII of this report, with special consideration for the young offenders, more frequent library privileges, and a simplified system of book distribution.
Then further recommendations were made regarding prison employment, and far reaching recommendations were made regarding amendments to the Criminal Code, rehabilitation and reports to sentencing judges.
June 18, 1965

Couple these recommendations, Mr. Speaker, with the general consideration I touched upon in my opening remarks, namely the fact that it is patently obvious in Canada today that there is a great lack of social welfare courts, social welfare judges, probation and parole officers. There is a great lack of the machinery needed to tackle the deep problems of juvenile deliquency. This we all know. We all know also about the major recommendations not of the Fauteux report but of the report to which I have referred, which recommendations are almost 30 years old. However, I support the setting up of this committee because I think it can deal usefully with some of the modern concepts which have come to light during the last 5, 10 or 15 years.
However, let this parliamentary committee not be an excuse for delaying action on the recommendations, not of the Fauteux report but of the Archambault report, one of the greatest royal commission reports in the history of this nation. If we do, Mr. Speaker, once more the Canadian public will have ample reason to become increasingly cynical about royal commissions and parliamentary committees. Because while the committee should and can do useful work, I hope I pointed out that what is really needed is action now, not tomorrow. We have no excuse for putting off action in these major areas of social and penal reform. Let us not kid ourselves about that, Mr. Speaker.
What is involved here is not a small amount of money. Millions and millions of dollars are involved. I can assure hon. gentlemen opposite, and I think I speak for Members in all corners of the House, that if they move forward in a real and dynamic way with the major recommendations of the Archambault report they will have the wholehearted support of Members in all corners of the House.
Some members of the Canadian public have the archaic idea that offenders should be thrown into old fashioned prisons and should stay there. On humanitarian and religious grounds alone this is not a very nice thing to say; but surely by talking about the rehabilitation of prisoners and the protection of society, and by the figures and statistics relating to recidivism, we have already shown that the system we have employed with such bad results for a number of decades has not worked at all. This is one instance where those of us who cry out, I think responsibly, for more reform should be listened to. I can assure the Government that if they move forward in this regard they will have our support.

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries
Again I say I am sure this committee will receive widespread support in the House of Commons as it gets down to work on some of the developments which have taken place in later years. But let us all get together and move forward now in areas of reform which for too long have been neglected.
[DOT] (1:00 p.m.)

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the notice of motion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) is most important, because it concerns the setting up of a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons to examine the question of penitentiaries coming under the jurisdiction of the Canadian government.
In 1946, when I was a young member-it does not mean that I am an old member now -in 1946, some members of the opposition and even some members of Mr. Mackenzie King's government spoke about setting up a committee to consider the situation of penitentiaries under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Parliament.
Then came the St. Laurent government, followed by the Conservative government, the Tory government, and every time, every year, every session, notices of motions were introduced to establish a committee to consider the penitentiary situation. We have been planning to consider this matter for 20 or 25 years and no solution has ever been found to settle this problem.
However, some people are considering the matter. We know that the situation existing in penitentiaries is being considered. Studies have already been made by experts in this field who concluded, as mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), that penitentiaries must be reformed in order to permit the rehabilitation of prisoners and convicts.
Penitentiaries could be greatly improved, made fit for occupation, or even more appealing, so that prisoners may be treated as human beings and not as animals.
We could, for instance, organize penitentiaries in such a way as to enable convicts to do some productive and useful work and it would be less costly for the government and the Canadian taxpayers to keep them in prison. Thus trade schools could be set up in penitentiaries to enable prisoners to learn a trade so that they would contribute to their rehabilitation after their release. But nothing is done in that regard.
June 18. 1965

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries
Since prisoners are also human beings, we could also provide penitentiaries with recreation halls, swimming pools, theatres, etc. to help inmates get good training and learn how to live decently in a normal world.
Earlier I heard a member of the N.D.P. say there was a law for the rich and a law for the poor. A great many things need to be reformed in addition to the penitentiaries to allow the rehabilitation of young people.
Not very long ago I had to do with two prisoners who were not convicts but two young men of 19 and 20 caught red-handed in a most reprehensible act. They were arrested in September 1964 and brought before the court, which decided to send them for trial. On account of the law's delays and its lack of organization, the trials may take place in October 1965 or in the spring of 1966. In the meantime, these two young men are in the Ville-Marie jail in Temiscamingue county. Bail has been set at $10,000, but the two men remain in jail because such an amount is not to be found on every doorstep. Those two young men have been jailed without trial; they are still waiting to appear in court because of the slowness of the judicial process in the province of Quebec.
Reforms are needed. There is a young man of 20 kept in jail pending his trial and from whom much too high a bail is requested. Because his parents cannot afford to put up bail, the young man stays in jail for a year, a year and a half, without having been sentenced to jail. And some think that the young man is thus being helped toward rehabilitation in society.
It is a flagrant abuse to treat 20-year olds that way, if we want to rehabilitate them; but if we could not care less, that is a different story; let us continue drifting in the same direction.
There is a great number of young men like those in the country. Once in jail, they are bored to death because practically nothing is organized to take care of them. They are left idle. If there was something for them to do in jail, I think that would greatly help them toward rehabilitation.
It is strange to see to what extent society is concerned about these people when, for instance, we read in the newspapers every day that a murder has been committed here or there, that hooded bandits have struck here or there, that gangsters are operating here or there, just to create sensation. But, when will the newspapers come up with a solution to make the rehabilitation of those young people easier? Wrongdoings are being 
emphasized but rehabilitation per se is not mentioned.
To a certain extent I blame the newspapers for making so much out of those things, of those murders here and there, of all those infractions, without ever coming up with a constructive answer. Circulation is the sole concern of some newspapers: to collect 7 cents or 10 cents per issue. Our young people are sacrificed in the name of all that publicity given to depravity.
It is time for the government to put an end to its motions for setting up fact-finding committees. The situation has been studied, considered and as the member for Brome-Missisquoi pointed out a while ago, the time has come to take action, to reorganize those penitentiaries, to revise our methods of rehabilitation with regard to our young Canadian prisoners or delinquents. They may be a bad lot, but still there is a little good in each and everyone of them. It is a matter of finding it and helping them toward rehabilitation, toward confidence in themselves. This confidence they can feel only when society makes it possible for them to do so. When that day comes our penal institutions will work constructively, enabling human beings to become once more honourable and reasonable.
We therefore express the wish that the government take action instead of being content with setting up fact-finding committees. We have had enough of committees. Let us act now and give our Canadians that to which they are entitled.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to intervene in this debate, but before saying that which I wish to say I should like to associate myself with the excellent speeches that have been made by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North, the hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi and the hon. Member for Villeneuve, who has just taken his seat. I think these were excellent speeches, and I should like to be associated with them.
[DOT] (1:10 p.m.)
The comment I should like to make, however, is that it seems to me the limited terms of reference contained in this resolution are in effect a reflection upon the Members of the House and the members of the other place. I cannot understand why, when this tremendously important subject of penitentiaries and penal reform is to be reviewed by a joint committee, the terms of reference should be
June 18, 1965

limited in the manner they are in this resolution. The resolution says that the subject matter referred to the joint committee is "to consider the state of penitentiaries .. .and the plans of the Government in relation thereto".
What is meant by "the state of penitentiaries"? To begin with, this is a phase which is virtually meaningless. I would assume that the "state of penitentiaries" meant a study of the buildings. Is it reasonable that Members of the House and the other place should form a committee and be asked to go into the sole matter of the buildings, and not into the far wider matters that are of great concern to the Members of this House?
As we well know, the Minister of Justice announced the terms of reference of a special committee on corrections, and in that connection the terms of reference include a study of the broad field of corrections in its widest sense from the initial investigation of an offence to the final discharge of a prisoner from imprisonment or on parole, including such subjects as arrest, bail, representation in court, conviction, probation, sentencing, training, medical and psychiatric attention, parole, pardon and so on. These are the broad, extensive and proper terms of reference that are given to this committee-a distinguished committee, it may be said, of people who are not Members of this House or of the other place.
But when it comes to asking Members of Parliament to look into this subject, the terms of reference are restricted to the state of penitentiaries. I do not suppose there is a single Member of the House who is not fully aware of the fact that the provision of buildings may be of importance, but it is of comparatively small importance compared with the wide number of matters referred to this outside committee.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: There is the question of staff.

subsubtopic: CONSIDERATION BY JOINT COMMITTEE OF SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext: For example, as the hon. Member for Vancouver East points out, questions concerning staff were raised in the House a month ago. Of far greater importance than the objective presumably set out in the resolution is the objective of assisting in the reform and rehabilitation of those who get into trouble, limiting the number of those who become repeaters, and making our whole penal system efficient as well as just in its application to those who have fallen afoul of the law. Yet what do we have here? The House is being asked to set up a joint committee with members of the other 22620-1671

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries place, and the members of this committee are to spend their time looking into the question of buildings and not deal with these broader questions.
It seems to me this is the wrong approach. I am satisfied that in all parts of the House there are Members perfectly capable of receiving information from those who are experienced in this field and then making recommendations to the House for effective action. Reference has been made to the Archambault report. I know a little about the Archambault report because Mr. Justice McRuer, then J. C. McRuer, was my senior partner and he spent about a year and a half with Mr. Justice Archambault as a member of that commission. They travelled all over Canada and Europe and made what has been described as a monumental report. They took a lot of time out of the lives of very busy and very competent men. They produced an excellent report but, as the hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi has told the House, many of the recommendations in that report have not been carried out yet. Why not? Because governments of the day were not ready to spend the money to do the things necessary to carry out the recommendations of that report. The same is true of the report of the royal commission headed by Mr. Justice Fauteux.
We do not need more outside commissions. It seems to me that if we are to get action on these things we need to solicit and arouse the support and the knowledge of Members of all parties in the House and in the other place so they will bring constant pressure to bear upon the Government to carry out some of these things that the experts suggest.
Is the report that eventually will be brought in by Mr. Justice Ouimet and his commission on these very same subjects to be pigeonholed like these other reports, and nothing done about it? I suggest that one of the ways to ensure that it cannot be pigeonholed is to have a committee of the House concerned with the broad range of this subject and determined, when these experts report, to see that what can be carried into legislation will be carried into legislation. It would be very much easier to do so if instead of Members making occasional speeches in the House, there was a continuing committee of those who over the years have qualified themselves particularly to deal with this subject.
Many other matters related to this question have come before the House from time to time. I myself brought in a resolution dealing
June 18, 1965

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries with legal aid in criminal cases. It seems to me that is the sort of matter that should be dealt with by a committee of the House. We have recently amended our rules of procedure, I think very wisely, to create a larger number of standing committees to try to elicit from Members of the House, be they backbenchers or whoever they may be and no matter to what party they belong, a more continuing attention to the various subjects that face Parliament and the people of Canada.
I have no doubt that this resolution will be passed because we are all in favour of it, but even at this late stage I would urge the Government to give serious consideration to enlarging the terms of reference of this committee so that all these vitally important matters may be looked into. I say "vitally important" not in terms of dollars and cents, although even in those terms our system is obviously wasteful and inadequate, but in terms of human lives that can be aided and assisted.
I think the machinery of the committee that will be created by this resolution ought to be used not just to inquire into something called "the state of penitentiaries", whatever that may be-I have not heard any representative of the Government explain what this drafting means-but to inquire into the same sort of broad field which has been included in the terms of reference of this other expert committee. That expert committee will only sit for the time being. No doubt it will make a particular report on some of the things that come before it. But I say it is the Members of the House of all parties who have a responsibility in this field, and I hope the Parliamentary Secretary and the Solicitor General will convey to the Government and the others concerned our view that the terms of reference here are unduly narrow and restrict the opportunities of those who will be members of this committee to make the real contribution of which they are capable in this field.

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that the Minister himself is not in the House, although I agree he cannot be here all the time. I think the establishment of this committee is very important, and in my opinion the Minister should be prepared to justify why a committee of Members of the House and of the other place is being established to give some direction with regard to the buildings and physical requirements of the penitentiaries
[Mr. Brewin.l
service. I suggest that probably the reason for the establishment of the committee is that a number of us had an opportunity to visit some of the prisons, and the reports we gave indicated a complete lack of modernization as well as conditions that would not be supported by the general public.
[DOT] (1:20 p.m.)
I am not sure, Mr. Speaker, whether this committee will serve any purpose. I am inclined to believe it will not if it is going to concern itself only with the building of penitentiaries. I believe the parliamentary committee will not be able to make any recommendations that will have any results for many years in the field of penitentiary construction. It is safe to say that the penitentiaries branch is much farther ahead in this field than Members of Parliament or the general public. The prisons we are building now, particularly in the third category, the minimum security category, are model type prisons. I believe also that the medium security institutions are not bad institutions in relation to the design and construction advocated by those who have been interested in penology for a long time.
I believe there is considerable difference of opinion in so far as maximum security institutions are concerned. It is in these institutions that the difficulty arises because, in many cases, men are confined to them for long periods of time. The abuses which took place, and which I presume led to the establishment of this committee, occurred in maximum security institutions. No one who is qualified to discuss this subject would disagree with the statements made by various people who have visited maximum security institutions, pointing out that they were a disgrace and something must be done.
One thing I find difficult to understand is that when we build new institutions, particularly of the maximum security variety, we do not place them in areas conducive to the work of rehabilitation. I believe it is generally agreed by all those interested in this subject that maximum security penitentiaries must be close to psychiatrists, psychoanalysts and others who work in that field. When a person is sent to a pen-tentiary it is not like sending him to take a course or putting him on a farm to enable him to become rehabilitated as part of society. I believe those concerned with maximum security institutions have to keep this in mind.
