Joint Committee on Penitentiaries
There is another committee that has been set up, and I think it is a very worth-while committee. I am in agreement with those who say that we in Parliament should not try to satisfy the public outcry that has occurred in recent months merely by establishing another committee. I agree that the Fauteux commission did a very good job, as did the Archambault commission when they investigated the whole penal system. They made recommendations that are probably as modern in terms of penal systems as any in the world today. They are still valid. However, the Government has done nothing about them.
This fact raises the matter of public apathy. I hope some other Members of Parliament have listened, as I have, in the last two days to a radio program in Ottawa called "The Open Line". This program has been discussing the problem of conjugal visits to penitentiaries. I raised this question in Parliament a number of years ago, and it resulted finally in a very good article in Chatelaine magazine. I was pleased that it should be given coverage in that type of magazine, because I feel it is a problem in which women are vitally interested and which affects women perhaps more than men, although women form a small percentage of our prison population.
I was interested in the discussion that arose from the Chatelaine article and which followed my introduction of the subject in Parliament, at which time I was hooted and told I was irresponsible. I have been interested in this radio program which during the last two or three days has been discussing the matter of conjugal visits, because it affects the whole penal reform system in Canada. I have been shocked and disgusted by the attitude of the Canadian people as indicated by this program. Many of them have said "Let us punish the prisoners. We did not send them there for a picnic; we sent them there to be punished". Why do these people not tell the Government that what they want to do is reinstate the beatings and the rat-infested prisons which we have tried to eliminate. These goody-goody people who have been on this program have talked about the Bible in terms of an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth; you steal a loaf of bread and you are put in prison for years.
I am shocked and ashamed of the people in Ottawa who have that attitude. These people have a right to adopt whatever attitude they wish, but I am shocked and ashamed of
them. All the reading I have done about prison reform indicates that even a backward country like Mexico goes much further than I would go. I believe that while we should rehabilitate the people in prison, we should not necessarily pamper them. I believe that advancement toward rehabilitation should be a reward, and that these visits of the family to the prison should be a reward.
The Mexican Government are more farsighted than we are because they view this as a right, not a reward. You do not give this as a reward for good behaviour; every prisoner, no matter how bad or what his crime or what his present condition or present attitude toward reform may be, is entitled to the same consideration. They even bring in prostitutes for the single people. They bring in girl friends if the girl friends want to go into the prison to visit their boy friends. They really repeat, on a limited scale, the type of relationship a person has outside, no matter what that relationship may be. I was interested in one of the questions which the radio announcer put yesterday to the woman who said you certainly could not bring prostitutes into a jail. He asked her whether she was aware of the homosexual problem in the jails and the lady said, yes, of course she was aware of it. He then asked whether, if her son were in jail, and if bringing in prostitutes would prevent her son being involved in a homosexual relationship, she would agree to such a course. She said: "If it was my son, I would certainly agree." I suggest that if it is good in an individual case the principle is good enough to deserve some consideration. [DOT] (1:30 p.m.)
I do not wish to leave the impression that I or those responsible for the operation of our penal institutions would go this far. I think we are a very backward nation, socially, and I do not think we are prepared to take this step. Most of us in this chamber are probably as backward as the average man or woman, and would not support it. The countries which have taken action of this kind have done so without much detriment to themselves or to the institutions, as far as I can find out. I would have expected nothing different.
I am pleased the officials of our own penitentiary branch have begun letting prisoners go home for two or three days. Recently this has been accepted by regulations and the Commissioner can now allow people to go home for as long as 15 days. The warden can grant leave of absence up to three days. These privileges have been granted for funerals and
June 18, 1965

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries recently they have been extended. I am still old fashioned enough to think we should use a system of this type as a reward to prisoners for accepting some of the benefits of rehabilitation.
I do not want to deal particularly today with the problem of homosexuals or the provision of facilities for conjugal relations in a prison cottage area. But I am sure anyone who is in his right mind would agree there is an advantage in extending privileges to prisoners while they are still under some degree of control by the institution. I can remember, when I was visiting St. Vincent de Paul talking to a young fellow who told me: I am not going to get into any trouble here, nor do I want to go out on parole or anything of that kind, because they have to release me in three months and as soon as I get out I am going to kill three people. I do not want anything to interfere with that plan.
Did you report that threat to the Department of Justice?

The Deputy Warden was there and heard what was said to me. There was nothing unusual about that statement. I believe he would have told the Warden-the man I think he was going to murder after he got out. I was particularly interested in not knowing. But after this man served his full sentence he would be set at complete liberty without the necessity for supervision or for working in co-operation with probation or classification officers. He need have nothing to do with them.
I think Members of Parliament should be concerned about these matters. On the other hand, I think the proposed Committee will be a waste of time if it is only going to design buildings and engage itself in architectural shenanigans in a field its Members know nothing about. It would be safe for me to say, for example, that we should double the size of the cells and instal better conveniences. As for the design of penitentiaries, that is another matter. I do not think the Committee will go to the trouble of finding out a great deal about systems other than those in use in North America. Maybe the Committee will go out to Saskatchewan where some architects have taken the drug LSD to help them design a mental institution-they took this hallucination producing drug so that they could put themselves in the position of the inmates and find out exactly what the inmates might prefer, and what would be most


conducive to their rehabilitation. If they were to do that, I think the committee would be "nuts". There is a better way of doing it and possibly we should allow the architects to continue to deal with these matters.
Does the hon. Member think we need take any drugs?

I am sure that Members of Parliament do not tend toward hallucinations, but they have other disadvantages. We are pretty backward in looking forward in terms of penal reform. The Minister himself has indicated that this is the case. In talcing this attitude we are probably doing no more than reflect the views of the public generally. When a matter affects them, it is one thing; when it affects someone else, it is something quite different.
I was interested in the similarity between two statements made on the radio program yesterday, one by a prisoner who had been in an institution for six years and another by a guard who had been a guard in a Federal penitentiary for a number of years. Each of these men adopted the archaic attitude that prisons must be tougher, that the food should be inferior and that conditions generally should be worse in order to assure the effectiveness of the deterrent. If this is the attitude of the public, obviously it will be very difficult to get anything done in the way of reforms. But I think Members of Parliament have an obligation to be more far-sighted than the public generally, and offer leadership in these fields. I do not believe the Government is giving any particular leadership, but I appreciate this fact: The more one gets to know the people in the Penitentiaries Branch the more credit must go, I think, to a Government of long ago which in a subtle way must have taken some of the expressions found in the reports of these various commissions and committees and applied them through the personnel in the Penitentiaries Branch. If Members of Parliament really knew some of the things which are going on in the penitentiaries they would be shocked, because I do not think they would be prepared to go as far as some of the officials have gone. I think these men should be congratulated on taking the chances they have taken in putting into effect measures of penal reform with which, I am sure, some Members of Parliament would not agree.
Another of the radio discussions concerned the birth of a child to a woman who had visited her husband in one of the penitentiaries. The public was concerned about this,
June 18. 1965

but its concern appeared to centre on who should be responsible for the support of the infant. Should it be supported by the province, which has responsibility for the maintenance of the family while the husband was in jail, or should it be the responsibility of the Federal Government because the Federal prison authorities had somehow turned their backs during the woman's visit? Surprisingly enough the public did not know that the Federal Government was in any case paying 80 per cent of the cost of caring for that family and for the child, no matter which authority might have to make the particular welfare arrangements. So the question of which authority would assume responsibility was largely hypo-, thetical. This program has thrown a good deal of light on public opinion, a factor which is often difficult to ascertain.
[DOT] (1:40 p.m.)
I think the Government should now give consideration to some of the things they have learned in this way. Perhaps it should sample public opinion in some way. If they did this, they would realize the crying need for this committee to have much broader grounds so that Members themselves would get some insight of our whole penal system and its operation. Then Members would have more knowledge of the operation of penal reform. They would be able to examine the results of some of the experiments that have already taken place in the federal penitentiaries system and the experiments that have taken place in countries more enlightened than ours. They would then have the opportunity and responsibility of building up public opinion to accept the changes that the Government is willing to accept and implement as soon as the people are willing to accept them.
This may not happen, Mr. Speaker. This Government is without doubt the most conservative, with a small "C", Government that I have seen for a long time. They want to establish a committee to do these things and they have taken the matter out of Parliament, so that Members of Parliament will only know the results when the report is brought in a number of years from now. I believe the Government has a responsibility to allow Members of Parliament to gain the knowledge that can be obtained from this committee. Members of Parliament would then have a responsibility to help develop public opinion. It is really not good enough to be willing, through the back door, to establish by regulation some of these things.

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries It is important that the public know what they are and are enlightened enough to demand the rehabilitation of prisoners.
I say this, Mr. Speaker, because it is a fact that if the prisoner returning to his community is not accepted by that community and cannot fit into the community again, he is not rehabilitated, no matter what has been done for him in a penitentiary in terms of readjusting his social and psychological outlook in order to solve the problem that put him into the penitentiary in the first place. You may correct this in the penitentiary; you may find that the classification officers indicate that rehabilitation is possible-but if you put this man into a community that will not allow rehabilitation, you really have not accomplished anything at all. I think the Government is being very narrow-minded and they are certainly very conservative in not allowing Members of Parliament to obtain a better insight of our whole penal reform system.
We should also talk about the guards. For many years we had, without doubt, the same type of guards in our institutions as we have had prisoners. You could change the uniform and put the prisoner inside and the guard outside, and as long as he could beat the prisoner or the prisoner could beat him it would not make much difference which one was inside the uniform. Keep the gates shut and keep the whole shooting match inside. One person went there voluntarily and the other was put there, but otherwise there isn't much difference between them. In recent years this has completely changed. This type of guard has not completely disappeared, but my experience is that we have a completely different type of guard today and we also have a completely different type of prisoner in many cases. They have become much smarter. I could name several prisoners who were considered to be almost uneducated but who were not uneducated at all. I am thinking of John Darrell Peters, or whatever his name is, who handled his case with great success all across this nation. His case has been in most of the Provinces; he has appealed and presented a highly documented legal case.
Is he any relation?

He is no relative of mine. I only learned of his case through the publicity we have received in this House on a number of occasions. I should also point out that I do not think he is a relative of the Liberal organizer who became notorious for bringing

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries his friends over from Scotland a few years ago. I only use him as an example. I think the guards have become smarter and the prisoners have become better educated because of the facilities which have been provided in our prisons.
I think the public should be aware of the other problems in this field. The hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) mentioned something that has always shocked me. I refer to the difference in sentences and the political orientation of the judge rather than a legal orientation. I might say that I have also had experience in court, but not on the same side of the fence as my learned friend from Greenwood. I have heard a magistrate say some of the things that the hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) mentioned. I can remember a magistrate standing up when he had to dismiss a charge against me and saying that there was no evidence to warrant a conviction or to justify the case going any further, but the work that I had been engaged in for the previous two months was, I think it was something like "nefarious and a disgrace to the nation". He used many other adjectives of that nature. I personally didn't think it was so bad; I had been a candidate for the C.C.F. at that time and was defeated two days before the trial by something like 500 votes. I had also been for some time a leader for the Steelworkers in a strike against the mining companies. I didn't think that was too bad, either. Personally, Mr. Speaker, I did not refer to the fact that the magistrate was secretary-treasurer of the mine that was having all the difficulty and really was not too impartial in any way, shape or form, as far as the whole mess was concerned.
Therefore I agree that justice should be dispensed equally and should be impartial and non-political. I have had quite a number of instances brought to my attention of persons being convicted who, if they had had any kind of lawyer to defend themselves, might have got off. These people have received very severe sentences simply because they were not defended. I remember the statement made by my hon. friend from Danforth (Mr. Scott), who said that there is nothing in the whole penal reform system or in the whole judicial system that can protect a person against a bad lawyer. This is perhaps a fairly strong statement, but I believe it is also fairly accurate. Often people involved in very serious crimes have to accept a young lawyer who knows absolutely nothing about the type of law he is

going to be presenting and has had absolutely no experience in that type of legal work. He may have articled with a legal firm doing a completely different type of work than that involved in the defence he has to put forward for some young criminal.
It is worse if they have an old lawyer who looks as though he might know something. That is more dangerous.

Mr. Speaker, could I ask the hon. Member a question? Is he going to support or oppose the setting up of this parliamentary committee?

Frankly, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it matters whether it is set up or not. I am not really much in favour of it. I am not opposed to it, if Members of Parliament can learn anything by discussing the blueprints for new prisons and their locations. I would like to ask the hon. Member who has asked the question not to forget what happened when politicians became involved in the new jail that was going to be built in Cornwall. This would probably highlight the situation as far as politicians are concerned and we would lose all the advantages expected from new penitentiaries. But this is only a vehicle to enable us to talk about some matters of penal reform which in my opinion would not even be considered by the committee.

Would the hon. Member permit another question. Can I ask the hon. Member for Timiskaming, who sits right behind me, whether he did not learn a lot about our penitentiaries system when as a Member of the House of Commons he visited penitentiaries and saw the conditions in them. Did he not think that if more Members visited these institutions and became interested in recidivism it might be of some value in making recommendations in regard to the subject of penology?

Yes; but I would also qualify my answer to the extent of saying that I also learned a lot more when I went around a penitentiary on my own than I did on two conducted tours. The only reason I learned very much about the penitentiary was because I consulted an inmate and he told me where I should go. The same is not true of a conducted tour, such as the one some hon. Members were taken on, a short while after my visit. In fact, the highlight of this tour was the statement made after the tour by the Minister.

Someone says you should spend some time in the pen to learn about it, but I have never found it that hospitable an institution to spend more than a day or two there. Personally, I think it would be pretty unnerving, even if you were a newspaperman, or as a Member of Parliament, to listen to all the noises at night in these institutions after the lights are turned off.
My real appeal to the Government is that they reconsider the limits they have placed on the terms of reference of the Committee and to broaden them. Matters such as parole, remissions, bail, supply of legal counsel, that very large and not well known field of the care of youthful offenders and their segregation in the whole judicial process from the time they are arrested until the time they are rehabilitated, the homosexual problem, permitting visits by wives of inmates, should in my opinion be brought before the committee so that immediate attention may be given to them.
I do not see why the Government should be scared of suggestions made by Members of Parliament on the basis of evidence available to them from former reports and the day to day operation of the new Committee which has been set up, unless, of course, the Government is of the opinion that the public is not ready to have the spotlight of public attention directed at these problems. If the Government, through this Committee, had a national program similar to the open line broadcasts over the radio, then in my opinion they would not find it nearly so hard to convince the public that changes do need to be made, rather than keep these matters in the dark.
I would see a Parliamentary Committee consisting of Members of Parliament and Members of the Senate turning the spotlight of public attention on problems which we think should be solved. If we only send Members of Parliament to prisons in order to examine them, each Member of Parliament will come back with an armful of smuggled literature and letters. And if they declare that they will return to the prison later, the supply of this material will increase tenfold. This will put a Member of Parliament into the position of judge and jury, causing him to make a number of decisions which I do not think he is capable of making.
That is not true.

My hon. friend says that it is not true. I suggest that for the last 20 years

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries or more he has been making such decisions and has become probably the best known friend of prisoners from coast to coast. In my opinion, this course of action has taken up a lot of his time and effort and on many occasions has brought him a lot of grief and heart searching. In closing I would ask the Government to give consideration to withdrawing this resolution and substituting one in much wider terms which will enable the Committee to look into the whole matter of penal reform. I should like to see a Committee set up to go into this whole question, be prepared to sit between sessions, to visit institutions in other parts of the country, to have meetings with the John Howard Society, the Elizabeth Fry Society, with universities connected with penitentiaries, with people connected with psychiatry, psychoanalysis, psychologists, sociologists, the judiciary, legal branches, Bar Associations, and so on. This committee would have the advantage of visiting these organizations and its Members would have a rounded out attitude toward what to do with any prisoner from the time he is arrested till the time he re-enters society.
It is my opinion that the average Canadian, if he is made aware of the problems in our penitentiaries, will be interested in the process of rehabilitation which must be the aim of our penitentiaries system. If we only lock people up and give expression to the belief of what I hope is a very limited number of people who consider penal institutions merely as a method of punishment, namely an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, and we are not able to convince the Canadian people that there is much more to the problem than this, then we have failed, and failed miserably.
If the Government broaden this Committee's terms of reference they will find great cooperation from Members on both sides of the House toward establishing the rehabilitation of those who have been guilty of offences. It is not good enough to say that those who are rich will receive consideration; those who are poor should also receive justice.
In closing I should like to refer to a letter I received yesterday which has caused me and a lot of other people with whom I have raised the matter a great deal of concern. It is in connection with the Nicholas case, a matter which I raised some time ago. Young Nicholas is quite happy with the fact that the Solicitor

Mr. Speaker,
I did not intend to take part in this debate, but as a practising lawyer, like others, I could not help being moved by the speech of the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin). The consideration and study of penitentiaries as they now exist is one thing which should be considered by a committee, but another committee should consider the whole question of penal reform. I have no doubt that the proposed Committee will consider plans for penitentiary buildings, and the present condition of penitentiaries, and will arrive at some conclusions as to what should be done. I think the hearings of this committee will provide an opportunity for members of the Civil Service in positions of administration to present their views and ideas in respect of improving our correctional system. The opinions of those people are valuable.
The proposed Committee will have the power to travel to see at first hand the conditions of our penitentiaries. I suggest that they should first travel throughout the municipalities and consider such things as day nurseries, the amount of money spent on day nurseries, and the number of working mothers which take advantage of such facilities, and relate that information to the incidence of crime. We should not close our eyes to the number of working mothers who

DEBATES	June 18, 1965
put their children in these day nurseries. This Committee should also consider Juvenile Courts in the various municipalities to determine how efficient they are and how qualified are their staffs. The committee should also go to the various schools in the municipalities and find out how many psychiatrists are assigned to assist in solving the problems of many of these school children. It is my understanding that one psychiatrist is available for about every 10,000 pupils. There is a tremendous shortage of psychiatrists in this field. This Committee should go to the law societies to find out how many lawyers, particularly younger ones, are interested in the problems of children and devote their time to these problems. Most lawyers are concerned about making money, and direct their talents toward corporation law because of the tremendous amount of money that can be made in that field.
This committee has the power to travel to these places and to carry out this kind of investigation, but whether or not they will do so is another question. I personally feel that they should make the kind of investigation I have suggested, rather than just a study of the bricks and mortar, so to speak. If they carry out that kind of investigation, I am sure they will truly understand the reasons behind the state of our penitentiaries and will find solutions to these problems.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that I was unable to attend to hear the speech of the hon. Member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin), as well as one or two others, but I did listen to several speeches made earlier which I felt were not relevant to the resolution before us. For instance, the speech made by the hon. Member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow), while it was very interesting and revealed one or two weaknesses in respect of the administration of justice in this nation, had nothing to do with the state of penitentiaries or the plans of the Government in relation to them as disclosed by the resolution now before us.
I enjoyed the speech of the hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) and I thought his points were very relevant, particularly when he suggested that the Government instead of appointing a new committee to carry out an investigation should implement some of the recommendations that have already been made. That is a suggestion that this House should seriously consider. There is no encouragement to Members of a com-
June 18, 1965	COMMONS
mittee, such as is proposed, in contemplation of the action that has not been taken by successive Governments in respect of the very excellent advice and recommendations that have been presented by various Commissions which have studied this whole question.
It seems there is always some reluctance on the part of Governments to push through penal reform in the face of public feeling that criminals are being mollycoddled. That feeling has been expressed in newspapers from time to time by responsible citizens and taxpayers. We have often heard the question asked, why is there this great concern for criminals; and I think that we as legislators have not pressed home the point often enough that we are not trying to make things easy for criminals, but trying to improve our correctional system so that prisoners who are released will not be convicted a second, third or fourth time and returned to the penitentiary. We should impress upon the public that in the long run money spent to modernize correctional institutions represents an investment that will save the taxpayers a great deal of money. We should sell that idea to the taxpayers of this country.
The statistics presented by the hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi clearly show that we have stalled long enough in our approach to this problem. Those statistics indicate that from 40 per cent to 70 per cent of all individuals sentenced to penitentiaries return a second, third or fourth time. If we want to protect the public and save the taxpayers' money, then we should adopt a correctional system which will reform prisoners so that following their release they become good citizens and do not again turn to crime. Surely that is the best protection that can be provided to the public. If that is not a good investment of public dollars, then I do not know what is, or how we could better spend the money on education.
Under the terms of this resolution this committee will be directed to consider only one aspect of the reformation of the administration of justice in this country. It is not directed to investigate the efficiency of our courts, how our provincial jails are run, whether there should be legal aid, and many other facets of this whole picture. I presume the Senators and M.P.s who are appointed to this committee will look at the physical buildings and facilities of our penitentiaries and study them from every point of view, including their capacity, their comforts or lack

Joint Committee on Penitentiaries the Committee is established, I submit there will be an obligation on the part of the Government to take action on the Committee's recommendations within a year at most after it reports. I have been a member of too many committees in the last three or four years which have made recommendations to the Government about which nothing has been done. I hope that will not occur in this case, and that the Committee will be able to meet, make a survey of a few penitentiaries and report soon so that quick action can be taken.

Mr. Speaker, since the government has decided to present this motion to set up a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons in order to consider the situation of penitentiaries under the jurisdiction of the federal government, I shall take a few minutes of the house's time to put a few remarks on record, particularly concerning the rehabilitation of prisoners after they leave the penitentiaries.
Like many others, I have noticed and deplored the fact that those who have served time in our penitentiaries are shut out from the federal, provincial and even municipal civil service.
What organization is in a better position to facilitate the complete rehabilitation of those who have served a few years in our penitentiaries? If the federal, provincial and municipal governments do not set an example in this field by accepting in the public service people who came out of penitentiaries, I wonder who will.
The time is past when such people were to be set aside because, in most cases, they did not intend to repeat their mistakes. They all deserve government help. Private concerns are not in a position to do that; neither are agencies, regardless of their good will, in the best position to co-operate in the rehabilitation of those people and in finding work for them so that they may continue to live as human beings. We have seen too many cases of people who have returned to crime simply because they did not find, in civilian life, any opportunity to work and earn an honourable living.
These are the remarks I wanted to put on the record. In that respect, I wanted to introduce a motion for debate. But when I noticed that the government had decided to submit this motion to the house, I felt I should make these few remarks; I also hope to have the opportunity of discussing the matter further

in committee. Besides, I intend to work on this personally and do my utmost to arouse interest, so that our governments might offer work to those who leave our penitentiaries after having served their time. Above all, I should like to see the Civil Service Commission and the government take the necessary means to ensure that these people can take courses while in prison, thus enabling them to prepare themselves for Civil Service exams.
I can see no problem here, and I know full well we can then feel, in conscience, that we have accomplished our duty with regard to the rehabilitation of these people.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOAN AND EXTEND REPAYMENT PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution concerns proposed amendments to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act which will extend the period during which guaranteed loans may be made to June 30, 1970, raise from $4,000 to $10,000 the maximum guaranteed loan amount which a fisherman may have outstanding, and increase from eight to ten years the maximum period over which loan under this Act may be repaid.
The purpose of the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act is to make bank and credit union loans more readily available to fishermen to help them finance a broad range of investment projects including the purchase, construction or improvement of fishing vessels, fishing equipment and shore installations. To this end, the Act authorizes the Minister of Finance to guarantee each lending institution
June 18, 1965

against loss up to 15 per cent of loans made aggregating $500,000. A guarantee of up to 10 per cent of total loans made is applicable in respect of loans made by that lender in excess of $500,000. There is an over-all limit on the total amount of guaranteed loans which may be made by all lending institutions, and this has been set at $20 million.
[DOT] (2:20 p.m.)
As the Act stands at present, the maximum loan amount is $4,000 and the maximum repayment period is eight years.
This legislation was enacted by Parliament in 1955 and was made initially effective for a period of three years. The period of operations during which guaranteed loans may be made was extended from time to time and this now expires on June 30, 1965.
The extent to which fishermen have made use of this credit facility has been fairly modest-I could add almost too modest to be really efficient-particularly when compared with the use that farmers have made of credit under the Farm Improvement Loans Act. Nevertheless, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act has proven to be a valuable supplement to other loan sources available to fishermen and, in some fishing areas, there has recently been an indication of growth in the use that is made of this facility.
Since inception to March 31 last year, close to 1,400 loans totalling $1.9 million were made. The upturn in lending is indicated by the fact that while annual loans until the fiscal year 1962-63 were in the $200,000 range, this increased to about $370,000 in 1963-64, and preliminary figures indicate that this trend continued into the 1964-65 fiscal year, during which loans may have come close to one half million dollars. Although the annual report for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1965, is not available, in fact during the period April 1 to December 31, 1964, the total loans made amounted to $340,000. This trend has been possible in large measure because of general improvements in fishing operations. These improvements, along with a trend toward the use of more costly equipment, also make it desirable to increase the maximum loan amount that a fisherman may borrow under the Act.
I should mention also that there have been significant changes in the fishing industry since 1955. These changes are now going on at an accelerated pace, and the most important of these is the expanding size of the individual fishing enterprise. Fishing, like agriculture, is becoming more and more
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act a business operation. Fishermen today must increase the scale of their operations, use larger vessels and more elaborate fishing gear if the fishing industry is to maintain its competitive position with other food producers. Similarly, increased efficiency and higher returns to fishermen must prevail if the industry is to survive in competition with other employment opportunities. My department is encouraging these developments in many ways through broad programs of research and development of new methods, subsidies on vessel construction and so on.
The proposed amendments to this Act fit into the total picture. I fully realize, Mr. Chairman, that this Act, as amended, is not going to meet all the credit requirements of fishermen and the fishing industry. I should like to refer particularly to its application to the Province of Newfoundland. As the annual reports will show, a small number of fishermen in Newfoundland have been able to take advantage of these loans. This is due to the fact that in a large number of settlements or communities there are no chartered banks and the fishermen have had little contact with banking institutions. We are looking into the possibility of finding more practical means of assisting Newfoundland fishermen in so far as making loans available to them.
In so far as fishermen are concerned, particularly in the meeting of their credit needs for larger and modern vessels and improved gear, I am a firm supporter of the provision of such credit through provincial fishermen's loan boards. This would explain, to some extent, why such a limited number of fishermen take advantage of this Act. Personally, I had a good deal of experience with the New Brunswick Fishermen's Loan Board and I can assure the House that a lending agency, which is close to the fishermen and close to the developmental possibilities of the industry, has much to commend it. I know this same conclusion has been reached in all the Atlantic Provinces where such provincial agencies have operated for many years. I am hopeful other Provinces will seriously consider similar action. I must add that following some of the federal-provincial meetings which have taken place with the inland Provinces and British Columbia in recent months, there has been an increasing interest in those Provinces in the possibility of establishment of Fishermen's Loan Boards. I believe there is a real possibility that this Act, as amended,
June 18. 1965

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act can be made to tie in closely with the operations of Provincial Loan Boards. There may well be many cases where loan boards can direct the fishermen to finance or credit unions, and thus relieve themselves of the necessity of tying up their limited capital resources.
In so far as the fish processing industry is concerned, I believe that the new program announced by the Prime Minister on June 7, whereby a newly established firm or expanding existing firms in designated areas will receive assistance from the Department of Industry, will go a long way toward meeting the needs of the fish processing industry. In this connection I should mention also the useful role of private capital from both domestic and foreign sources. The fishing industry is now enjoying a strong market, both at home and abroad, and is generally in a healthy, expanding condition. Under these circumstances the credit needs tend to increase, but at the same time credit becomes more easily available.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, the proposed amendments are simple and direct. They will extend the period during which guaranteed loans may be made as well as increase the extent to which an individual fisherman can use this credit source. As a result, fishermen will have a more ample opportunity for borrowing, on reasonable terms and conditions, to meet their growing capital needs. This, together with other measures taken by the Government, by the Government in collaboration with the Provinces, and by the Provinces, will in a modest way further contribute to the improvement of efficiency and the expansion of a very important primary industry.

speechtext:
First, I wish to express to the Minister of Fisheries my appreciation for the concise and objective statement he has made on this matter. As he said, the Act which this bill will amend, introduced and passed in Parliament in 1955, was extended in 1959 for another three years, and amended at that time to expand the definition of those who could borrow under it; and it was again extended in 1962. This is another extension and I agree with the proposal that the Act should be extended for five years, this time, instead of for three. I think it is unnecessary that an Act of this sort should come up for review as frequently as every three years.
I am pleased, also, to note that the ceiling on loans is to be raised from $4,000 to

$10,000. This will not, in my judgment, bring about an increased use of this legislation in proportion to the increase in the ceiling, but it is a step in the right direction and it may cover a number of cases which were not covered by the Act previously. If for no other reason, the tremendous increase in the cost of fishing equipment since 1955 is sufficient justification for raising the ceiling to a considerable extent. As a matter of fact, I want to say at once that we in this party will support this amendment. We may have certain suggestions to offer as we go on, but we will support it.
As the Minister has told us-and this was my experience, too, as Minister of Fisheries -this Act has not been used by fishermen to the extent we had hoped. It was introduced as a companion piece of legislation to the Farm Improvement Loans Act. But in some areas at least fishermen have not used it to the extent that farmers have used the corresponding legislation. There are a number of reasons for this, of course. The obvious one is that fishing gear has to be insured because it may very well be lost. There is much less risk of this happening to farm implements. Then again, fishing equipment can wear out rapidly and a condition could develop whereby it would all have to be replaced at one time, whereas farmers can add to their equipment year by year.
However, this does not provide us with a full explanation why the Act has not been used as much as we had hoped. There must be other elements-inaccessibility of lending institutions, for example, or the question of getting into the habit of financing fishing operations by this means. In Prince Edward Island the legislation has been used proportionately a great deal more than in other provinces. The population of that Province is only about one half of 1 per cent of the total population of the country. Nevertheless, the fishermen of Prince Edward Island have taken out 35 per cent of the loans granted under this legislation for the whole country, and the volume of the loans taken out on the island is more than 25 per cent of the whole. Had commensurate use been made of the Act in the rest of the country, total loans would have been several times greater than has in fact been the case.
I suggest to the Minister that he continue to try to find ways of encouraging fishermen to use the benefits available under this Act to a greater extent. We are living in a very competitive age and it is good business for
June 18. 1965

fishermen, if they are in an economically sound situation, to make use of as much credit as they can. As long as their operation is efficient they can make it more efficient by equipping themselves to carry out their work properly.
I do not think there is anything else 1 wish to say, except that I am pleased to note the Minister holds the view that the provinces also have a large responsibility in this field. I notice that a contrary view was expressed by the Opposition critic on the last occasion this Act was amended. My view is in accord with that of the present Minister. Three years ago, when this Act was last considered, the Opposition critic of that day, now Minister of Transport, said as reported in Hansard of March 6, 1962 at page 1546:
I am sure the hon. Member for Royal, the Minister of Forestry, would agree with me when I say that the plain fact is that this is not something that ought to be left to provincial governments. Under the constitution fisheries are the exclusive responsibility of this parliament and the Federal Government. Surely if farm credit, when agriculture is a joint responsibility of Parliament and the legislatures, is largely assumed by Parliament, credit for fishermen should be the responsibility of this Parliament.
I do not agree with him and I hold the same view as the present Minister in this connection. I think his conclusion is based on sound reasoning and his experience in the Department.
I have nothing more to say at this moment. We may have some further remarks to make as representatives of this party, and there may be some comments by other hon. Members, but it is not our intention to prolong the debate at this stage.

Member for Queens, I usually find presentations made by the Minister of Fisheries disarming if one does not look beyond the content of the statements he makes in such a pleasant manner to the House. Unfortunately, all too often when the Minister of Fisheries presents a resolution of this kind, a relatively minor amendment to a relatively minor piece of legislation, he is something of an orphan within the Federal Government, carrying far less weight in its councils than the Minister of Finance, who is also directly concerned with the bill we now have before us for consideration.

I must say, Mr. Chairman, that when I thought about the fact that we might be considering this resolution fairly soon, my mind went back to a year ago last January when
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act we had a Federal-Provincial Fisheries Conference in Ottawa, an event which was heralded as being something of major significance to the fishing industry of Canada and was going to usher in a new era of national fisheries policy. When I look back over what has happened in Parliament since that time, this would appear to be the second matter dealing with the fishing industry, as far as my recollection goes, that has come before the House since that time. The other matter that did come before the House had to do with the extension of our territorial fishing zones. Here again, the impact of that piece of legislation has been really of very little consequence to date.

The net result of that piece of legislation has been perhaps to lull the people of Canada who maybe have not much acquaintance with the fishing industry into thinking that the present Government has proposed and accomplished something significant in the fisheries field, when in point of fact they really have not done very much except set up in the House a piece of window dressing legislation.
Now we have a proposal to make a modest revision to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act which will increase the total which can be borrowed, from the great sum of $4,000 to $10,000, which is the maximum for any one loan, which will provide for a small extension of the repayment period and renew this program for another five years. I think we have to consider this resolution in the context of the present picture. The Minister will recall that when the Premier of Newfoundland presented the brief of the Government of that Province to the Federal-Provincial Conference he laid before it, with

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act some emphasis, a letter he had received from the present Prime Minister when he was Leader of the Opposition, in which the Prime Minister assured the Premier of Newfoundland that we would have a national fisheries program which would parallel what had been done and what would yet be done in the field of agriculture. Yet, as I say, this is only the second piece of fisheries legislation which has been put forward. I would also suggest, Mr. Chairman, that surely no one on the opposite side of the House would wish to claim that the proposal advanced in this resolution is any major step toward creating a program for the fisheries that parallels the program in respect of agriculture.
At the beginning of last session we had a Speech from the Throne, as we usually do at the beginning of a session, and then we had a speech from the Prime Minister after the Leader of the Opposition had spoken. In that debate of a year ago last February the Prime Minister, as I recall it, delivered himself of some rather extensive remarks. Having listened to the Prime Minister rather carefully and having just prior to that sat in on some of the sessions of the Federal-Provincial Fisheries Conference, I was awaiting with a good deal of interest some expansion by the Prime Minister on the brief reference in the Speech from the Throne to the development of a fisheries program. The fact was that during the whole of his speech, which went on at some considerable length, as I have said, the Prime Minister never once mentioned fish or the fisheries. On February 21, 1964, as reported at page 91 of Hansard for that session, I asked the Prime Minister the following question:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. In his speech yesterday the Prime Minister made reference to broadening and expanding the scale of farm credit. He made no reference to the fishery. I should like to ask him what measures he has in mind to parallel this action as far as the fishery is concerned.
Hansard records that Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister) replied:
Mr. Speaker, I am very conscious of the fact that I did not mention fisheries in my statement yesterday. It was an omission, but I can assure my hon. friend that assistance to agriculture in the form of broadening the basis of farm credit and in other ways will certainly be paralleled by help to the fishery.
As I say, that was on February 21, 1964, and as far as I know from that day until this the Prime Minister has never said anything in this House about a new national


fisheries program. The resolution which we have before us is the first definitive action proposed in this Parliament, as far as I can recall, since February 21, 1964, when the Prime Minister gave me that answer, that could even remotely be considered to be creating a parallel program for the fishery. I am convinced that fishermen will be very proud and satisfied with this measure granting them an extension of 8 to 10 years to repay loans and increasing them from $4,000

to $10,000. This is a first step taken by the government.
On the other hand, the true problem would be to find a market to guarantee the sale of their fish. If fishermen must borrow to buy some modern fishing equipment in order to improve their efficiency and if they are not sure that they will sell their entire catch, they will always hesitate to do so. Such is the problem in the Gaspe peninsula at present. Fishermen have signed a contract with the United States who set and control the price of fish. Recently, the Quebec Minister of Fisheries was approached by the government of Haiti in order to enter into a contract for $3 to $5 million worth of fish. They were told there was a shortage of fish and that the small catch along the Gaspe coast was used solely to fill orders from the U.S., since they hold an exclusive contract.

In addition, several countries would be interested in dealing with us, but our governments do not seem to care. They should look after the marketing of our surplus fish; this would provide the industry with some profit and the fishermen with a certain amount of security; under those conditions they would equip themselves so as to make the largest catches possible; but, without that assurance that they can sell all their production, they will not be interested in obtaining loans and getting further into debt.

Having said that, I must point out that I was glad the Minister himself recognized the fact that this legislation will not be of any material benefit to the people of my riding, and I doubt that it will be of very much benefit to the fishermen of Newfoundland generally.
Some Members have attributed this to the lack of banks. It is true that we have very few branches of chartered banks in the smaller fishing communities of Newfoundland. In my own riding there are six. Two of them are quite close together on the Burin peninsula and the others are scattered along a coastline that extends for nearly 1,000 miles. But that is not the main reason. Even in those communities where banks are readily accessible
DEBATES	2633
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act the fishermen cannot make any use of this legislation mainly because the bank managers, for some reason which I have not been able to fathom, are very reluctant to make loans to fishermen even though the loans are guaranteed by the Government.
I think the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni said that up to the time the Dominion-Provincial Conference was held a year ago 12 loans had been made in Newfoundland amounting in total to $19,000. Two of those loans were made in my own riding, and I know about them because I know they would never have been made if I had not personally underwritten them. Therefore this amendment will not improve the situation so far as Newfoundland fishermen are concerned.
The Minister said he was disappointed that fishermen had not made more use of this legislation, but I was glad to hear him say that this is changing and fishermen are gradually making more and more use of it. I presume that is the reason for the extension of the maximum amount of loan. As I listened to the Minister I was struck by the similarity between this legislation and the legislation placed on the statute books several years ago making provision for loans to small businesses. I think the Minister said that the total amount of loans made under this legislation would not exceed $20 million. The same thing has happened in the case of small business loans. So far as my riding and province are concerned, that legislation has not served the purpose for which it was intended.
We in Newfoundland would be quite happy with smaller loans, even less than $4,000, if they were obtainable but, as I said, we have so few banks and no credit unions and the banks are not accessible to fishermen. They are hundreds and hundreds of miles distant. The only way to get to them is by sea, which is expensive and can take a lot of time. So it is just impossible for the fishermen to make any use of the legislation.
I was glad to hear the Minister say that some other provision would have to be made to take care of the problem in Newfoundland. We need small loans to look after special needs. In Newfoundland we have the inshore fishery and the deep sea fishery. The deep sea fishery is taken care of under the shipbuilding program and the measures to which the Minister referred in his interjection in the remarks of the hon. Member for Comox-Alberni. But so far as the inshore fishery is concerned, it is not in the fisherman's interest to saddle himself with a huge amount of
2634	COMMONS
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act debt. The smaller he can keep the capital investment, the better. In my opinion it should not exceed $5,000 per person and the maximum of $10,000 should preferably be divided among two or three persons.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
What we need in Newfoundland is a loan fund that will take care of emergencies. A fisherman may need a new boat. He can go into the woods and cut the timber for the frame but he needs some ready cash, $400 or $500 or perhaps $1,000, to buy planking for the hull and deck. If he has a boat, it is probably in his interest to get one of the small diesel engines that are now available on the world market. These little engines range in power from 5 horsepower up to 15 or 20 horsepower, but usually from 5 to 10 horsepower. They cost anywhere from $500 to $800. There should be a fund to which the fishermen can go to secure that amount of money. He is not saddled with a great amount of debt, and he is in a fair position to repay it over a short period.
Last winter one of my fishermen fishing with a longliner suddenly had $1,000 worth of gear destroyed by a foreign trawler. Well, this was a tremendous loss. He could not go to the bank because he had no more security to put up to satisfy the bank. He had to do without this gear until a merchant or a plant operator provided him with it. Only last week I had a letter from a constituent who said he could make a fairly good living if he could get a fleet of nylon gill nets. He has not been able to afford to get them up until now. These nets can be purchased through a Government agency for about $50, and can be put into the water for perhaps $75, fitted with moorings, floats and everything. He needs the cash, and he does not have it. The only other alternative for him is to purchase these nets through a supplier, but instead of paying $50 for the nets he will pay $100 or perhaps $120, exclusive of the moorings. These are examples of the needs which our fishermen want met.
The trouble with this legislation is that it does not help the people who most need help. If a person can go to a bank and get a loan of $10,000 under this legislation, he does not need the legislation. He could likely get the $10,000 loan anyway. It is the poor fisherman who has no security to offer except his good name, his industry and his reputation as a fisherman, who needs the help. Somebody has to take him at his face value and advance money on his character.

DEBATES	June 18, 1965
Now, we have two loan funds in Newfoundland. We have the Fisheries Development Loan Fund, and that fund is used mainly for large loans for fishermen who want to buy Danish seiners. I do not believe that fund has been successful at all. What has happened has been this: A fisherman goes to this loan fund and obtains a loan of $40,000 or $45,000 to build a Danish seiner of about 75 feet. This is a tremendous amount of debt. Along with that, the marine insurance on this ship is very high and the operating expenses are high. By the time this man pays off his loan, he is right back where he started. He catches more fish, but he is no better off. The extra production goes to pay off the loan.
The most successful arrangement we have had in my Province has been a little fund that originated when the Premier of Newfoundland sold the Newfoundland Savings Bank to the Bank of Montreal. About $1 million was produced from that sale and it was split into two funds, half for the farmers and half for the fishermen. The purpose of the fund was to grant small loans to fishermen. There was a limitation as to what they could buy. They could buy only those types of gear and build those types of boats which met Government specifications. However, this fund could not begin to satisfy the demand. The amount of the loan was limited to less than $1,000. I think the average loan would be about $450.
Now, this legislation will not touch that need at all because the person who needs the help is not in a position to take advantage of it. I do want to appeal once more to the Minister. This legislation is all right. It will help somebody, and we will support it. However, so far as my Province is concerned and so far as my riding is concerned, we want a different form of financing. I hope the Minister will see to it that a fishermen's loan fund will be set up. I disagree with the hon. Member for Queens when he says this should be a provincial responsibility. I do not see why it should not be the responsibility of the Federal Government to provide this form of help to the fishermen, just as the Federal Government aids the farmers. We have more or less committed ourselves to do as well for the fishermen as we do for the farmers. I do hope the Minister will tackle this problem without any further delay.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE AMOUNT OF LOAN AND EXTEND REPAYMENT PERIOD
speechtext:
It is not my intention to speak at any great length or delay unnecessarily the passage of this resolution. I listened with great interest to the remarks of the hon.
June 18, 1965

Member for Burin-Burgeo. I could not help but note, with amazement, the marked similarity between the difficulties which face the inshore fishermen in Newfoundland and those which face our inshore fishermen in Nova Scotia. I dare say this is true of the entire Atlantic Provinces. The senior Member for Queens, and former Minister of Fisheries, stated that the Official Opposition's position is to approve of this resolution, and with that observation I concur.
The resolution before us states:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act to increase the maximum loan amount to a fisherman from four thousand dollars to ten thousand dollars and to increase the maximum repayment period from eight years to ten years and also to extend the period during which guaranteed loans may be made for a period of five years from June 30, 1965 to June 30, 1970.
Obviously, if this Act were going to be used at all the amount of the guaranteed loan had to be increased and the repayment period extended, especially in view of constantly rising costs. This is a very minor piece of legislation. It has not been, since the date of its inception, very beneficial to fishermen. In fact, many fishermen and bankers as well are apparently unaware of the existence of the Act. It is my understanding that the original purpose of this legislation was to facilitate the provision of term loans to fishermen, credit was being made available to finance a broad range of investments including the purchase, construction or improvement of fishing vessels, fishing equipment and shore installations. It was introduced in 1955 for a period of three years. The Government indicated at that time it would undertake to reimburse individual lending institutions for losses up to 15 per cent of loans or an aggregate of $500,000. A guarantee of 10 per cent is applicable in respect of loans, and that is not to exceed $500,000. There is an over-all limit of $20 million on the total amount of guaranteed loans which may be made by all lending institutions.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
This Act was amended in 1959 and again in 1962. This resolution therefore represents the third time on which the Act has been amended or extended since its introduction. I simply note that the Minister has decided that the period of the guaranteed loan would be extended for another five years, or until June 30, 1970. I agree with this move. I do not see why this Act should come before Parliament every three years. However, it is

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act evident that since its inception this legislation has met with only modest acceptance among the people it was designed to benefit. The number of loans granted makes this clear. In fact from the time of its inception in 1955 to March 31, 1964, a total of only 1,379 loans have been made, amounting in value to approximately $1,916,727. During this period a total of 281 loans were made in Nova Scotia to an amount of $392,248.
It is interesting to see for what purpose these loans were made. Loans for fishing equipment accounted for 365, to a value of $403,122. There were 1,003 loans in respect of the purchase or repair of vessels and boats, the total being $1,493,883. Eleven were in respect of the building and construction of vessels totalling in value $19,722. It is therefore evident that this Act has not been very beneficial to our fishermen or to the industry. It seems to me that some major improvements should be brought about which would make this legislation more attractive and more adapted to the needs of our fishermen. Last year only 202 loans were made, to a value of $368,229. Of the total number of loans made since the inception of this scheme, 897 amounting in value to $1,284,142 have been repaid. It is interesting to note that only three claims amounting to $615 have been paid by the Government since the inception of this Act.
A study of the small pamphlet put out by the Department of Fisheries covering the terms of this Act may well explain the reason for its lack of popularity. For example, it offers the fisherman no solution to his problem in time of disaster, and if he should lose his boat and fishing gear, which are not always adequately insured, he is not in a position to make the down payment for a new boat which is required by the chartered banks. I believe the amendments proposed, though beneficial, do not go far enough, and I think the government should give more consideration to the needs of our inshore fishermen when introducing amendments to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. After all, our inshore fishermen are still a vital factor in the economy of the Atlantic Provinces. Our lobster fishermen, for example, still top the list in dollar earnings and their catch generally represents 30 per cent of our province's landed value, which in 1964 was in excess of $42 million. The total catch for the Atlantic Provinces was 45 million pounds, worth $20 million.
Lobster fishing is one phase of the fishing industry which remains in the hands of the
2636	COMMONS
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act primary producer, and one can safely say that it is the prime factor in keeping alive the inshore fishing industry along the entire coast line of Nova Scotia. Lobstering is usually a two-man partnership. Sometimes it is a father and son business, with each sharing equally in the profits and the losses. There are also some fishermen who like to go it alone. The lone fisherman is typical of the lobster fishery. Rugged and independent, he represents a way of life where a man is his own boss and where one's reward depends on the sweat and toil put into the job. Certainly this is no nine-to-five job. When I am at home in Lunenburg I am sometimes awakened by the loud exhaust of the lobster fishermen's boats as they put out to sea around four o'clock in the morning to haul in their traps. These sturdy individualists are representive of the fibre and sinew of this nation and they have truly earned the title of primary producers.
When the weatherman is kind and the sea gives up its red treasure, these inshore fishermen seek no help from anyone. But when disaster strikes and their meagre resources are inadequate to enable them to replace their boats and equipment they must turn to someone for help. This happens all too frequently. Last year, 39 fishermen were lost in the Maritimes, the greatest single tragedy being the loss of the trawler Acadia Sea Hawk when Captain Ronald Mosher and his crew of 13 men vanished beneath the shroud of a wintry Atlantic storm. Other than those aboard the Sea Hawk, the death toll involved mostly inshore fishermen. Inshore fishing accidents happen frequently and only a few months ago we read in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald how Keith Dixon and his 17-year-old son narrowly escaped death when a gasoline tank aboard their Cape Island type motorboat exploded at Woods Harbour, Nova Scotia. The boat-only three years old-was badly damaged by fire.
How will this legislation help these people? Oh, the Minister may say, they can get a loan under this Act to replace their boat and equipment. Let us look at the pamphlet and see what security they need. In the section dealing with security for a loan the pamphlet states the requirements to be:
(a)	A promissory note signed by the fisherman and endorsed by one or more financially responsible persons, or
(b)	Security on an insured fishing vessel...
(c)	If the principal amount of the loan is $1,000 or less, an assignment of moneys to be paid to the fisherman.
Let us suppose no one will sign this note. His boat is destroyed and his earnings without

DEBATES	June 18, 1965
equipment are negative. How does this fisherman get re-established? Would not a personal life insurance policy for the amount of the loan or the equity in a home be acceptable security? The Act is not clear on this point.
In the first part of the pamphlet the Department defines those who make application for a loan. It lists a fisherman as one who has a legal interest in a fishing vessel or a fish trap, and who intends to gain his livelihood from catching fish for sale. Many of today's fishermen find it difficult to qualify under this section of the Act, since they may not own shares in ships. I think a fisherman could also be defined as one who spends three or more months at sea, and whose unemployment insurance book contained sufficient stamps to verify this fact. The only real benefit under this Act at present is the 5 per cent interest rate on any loan that may be secured. However, when all the factors facing our inshore fishermen are taken into consideration, this is truly a very small concession.
If the Department is desirous of really assisting our inshore fishermen I would suggest it give more consideration to their real needs. In order to do this, conferences or consultations should be held in those areas where large numbers of our people are engaged in fisheries. The views of these men should be noted by our departmental experts and conveyed to our naval architects, our ship and boat builders and our engine and equipment suppliers, so that every aspect of improvements in small fishing craft could be studied. This could well bring about a more satisfactory and efficient design of inshore craft which the Department of Fisheries could approve, and which would then be more acceptable as collateral for a loan when any inshore fisherman desired a new boat or a replacement boat.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest that the amount of any loan approved, and which is guaranteed by the Government, should be supported to a greater extent by the Government than at present, especially when the fisherman suffers a major loss. A Government guarantee of a minimum of 25 per cent repayment on the loan would be a suitable amendment to this Act, especially when a fisherman loses his boat and all his equipment in a storm or major disaster. I hope the Government will give careful consideration to these proposals and implement them in this bill, or in the not-too-distant future.
June 18, 1965	COMMONS

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome the opportunity of joining those who have spoken on this resolution. 1 might add that, like the other speakers, I am pleased to see the broadening of this particular Act with a view to making it applicable to a greater number of the needs of fishermen. I am especially interested, however, in the needs of the inshore fishermen in the immediate future. Had I the time, Mr. Chairman, I would talk about some other aspects of the fisheries development program, such as the centralization program, the legislation for the 12-mile limit, and so on; but the fisheries development program of necessity is a complex one and deals with many facets of the fishing industry from the time before the fish is even caught up to the time it is sold. Such a program has to be far reaching; it will take time to get into full effect, and is one which will require the efforts of many officials both federal and provincial.
In the interim, however, the productivity of fishermen must be increased. I cannot think of a better way to get immediate results so that the incomes of fishermen can be improved than making available loans for those fishermen who need to improve their boats and gear, to improve their shore installations, and beyond that, to assist those men who perhaps are not fishermen now or who at one time were fishermen and want to return to the fisheries but do not have the boats, gear or money and must obtain capital assistance in order to become fishermen.
Without doubt, Mr. Chairman, capital assistance can be of immediately help to fishermen who wish to improve their existing equipment. A fisherman may require a new engine; he may want to make repairs to his boat, to his fishing gear, his traps or his trawls. When he is able to borrow the money for these things he is immediately equipped to produce more efficiently and to improve his income. I cannot think of a better way, with the possible exception of a further extension of the bait service, to immediately permit an increase in the income of fishermen than the provision of a means whereby fishermen can obtain capital assistance.
Like other speakers, Mr. Chairman, I wish to register by approval of the resolution and express the hope that fishermen will use this legislation. I also express the hope which has already been expressed by previous speakers, namely that the Minister of Fisheries will determine the necessity of making available to fishermen the capital assistance with which
DEBATES	2637
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act they can immediately become more productive and thereby earn better incomes. I was very glad to hear the Minister say that he had in mind the Province of Newfoundland with respect to the availability of loans under this Act. I have no doubt that the Minister will take whatever steps are necessary in order that there will be greater use made of this Act by the fishermen themselves. I do not wish to unduly delay the passage of this legislation, Mr. Chairman, and will conclude simply by reiterating the fact that there is perhaps no better way in which fishermen can immediately improve their position than taking advantage of capital assistance.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to deal with one specific problem in connection with this matter. I would certainly like to compliment the Minister of Fisheries upon the step he has taken in increasing the scope of the loan and the amount of time given to the borrower to repay that loan. The problem I wish to discuss concerning loans is one that is perhaps bothering the Minister as well. I believe he is very familiar with it, because it is not a new problem. It is the fact that with regard to the inland fisheries and the fishermen I have the honour to represent, although there are grants, subsidies and loans made available at the federal level, for some unexplained reason it seems impossible for these loans to be made available to inland fishermen to the same degree that they are available to the coastal fishermen.
Only yesterday in the lake port of Wheatley there was a meeting of fishermen, the processors and the provincial Department of Lands and Forests which dealt with this very problem, namely the inability of local fishermen to take advantage of federal provisions. I would like to ask the Minister- and I listened with great interest when he discussed the fact that federal-provincial boards were being set up-because of his awareness of this problem, is there some way in which a meeting or an investigation could be held here in the Province of Ontario to see if it is not possible to work out a way in which the local fishermen could be placed on the same basis as coastal fishermen, as far as loans are concerned? It could well be that because there is no Department of Fisheries in Ontario and the fisherman must make representation to the Department of Lands and Forests, the vehicle is not present whereby such action can be taken. If such is the case, I think we should know it and
June 18, 1965

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act know it now, so that the appropriate steps can be taken to remedy this ill.
I know that when the fishermen of that area speak of not being able to obtain these loans, subsidies and grants, they are stating the fact, because I have been to the previous government and this Government with these fishermen to discuss their problem in detail. I have found the departments here very sympathetic in regard to the problems of the local fishermen and wishing to do all in their power to help these men, but they have been unable to find the mechanics for so doing. I have made representations to the provincial department and found there, too, sympathy for the problems of these fishermen, but they also seem unable to find an avenue of approach.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I would like to ask the Minister if he will give me a specific undertaking that he will look into this matter and see whether it is not possible from now on to put the local fishermen, the inland fishermen, on the same basis as far as loans, grants and subsidies are concerned as the fishermen on either coast. Because there is very little value in increasing the amount of loans or increasing the time to repay them if the local inland fishermen are not in position to take advantage of them.
The Minister has said that the amount lent so far is modest. He said he was disappointed at the use made of them. Perhaps the solution would be a concerted effort on the part of all parties to see why this is so, and whether something can be done at the earliest possible moment to widen the use of these loans. Farmers in my area have derived much benefit from the companion loans under the farm improvement loans legislation; these loans are used to a tremendous degree by local farmers. I would ask the Minister what can be done, either by working through the provincial fishing bodies or directly, to see that the local fishermen, the honest, hard working men who are facing grave problems today, are not placed in a position where they cannot receive the necessary funds to carry on their business, which I am sure they would be glad to do if given every opportunity.
