speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I apologize for delaying the Committee a little; I know the mood of the Committee is to get on with the business this afternoon. Perhaps the only thing of significance which will be said of my speech when I sit down is that it will

probably be longer than the Gettysburg address.
May I say first of all that were it not for the inclusion in the remarks of the Minister of an awareness of the lack of application of this Act, then I would find it very difficult to support this resolution. I think this Act is a great illustration of the mentality of many people who perhaps are in charge of rationalizing certain programs to make them acceptable to the standards of a mysterious class of people. This is an orthodox bill because it implies that the fishermen can get assistance by going to a bank. The fact that the legislation does not work is not, I suppose, of very much concern to some of those who have more the mentality perhaps of an accountant rather than that of an economist or sociologist, and it is a neat little package.
In the past two years the Minister has made aware to those of us who realize the inadequacies that he is fighting to do something about them. I am not going to eulogize the accomplishments of the past two years; I have done that on many occasions and I do not deem it necessary to do so at this time. However, I would say that he has probably been the most successful Minister of Fisheries on record. It is a tough job, particularly when dealing with the province of Newfoundland.
A lot has been said about our small boats and our inshore fishermen, who comprise 95 per cent of the Newfoundland fishermen. I think we must admit that the coming thing in fisheries is our off-shore fisheries. When we are talking about our inshore fishermen, we must realize more and more that our fishermen will become involved in our offshore fishery either on trawlers or in fish plants.
Once again I say there are forces at work in this country which would impede this development. There are already a number of successful operators in Canada who have managed to be successful in fishing enterprises. They are not particularly concerned about attracting new industry or fishing companies to develop the resources of the Atlantic Provinces. It is a great tragedy to witness so much activity by foreign countries off our shores, who send their boats to take the fish. While those few companies which do operate in the Atlantic provinces do well it seems to me that the real answer is to get some of these companies who are operating in Europe to operate off our shores through a Canadian subsidiary, thus developing our fishing industry.
June 18. 1965

There are those who are quite concerned about Canadian ownership, and I subscribe in many instances to the view they hold. But it does seem to me that any study of the fishing industry makes us aware of the fact that there are a few major companies in Europe who are now sending many of their ships to the Atlantic coast of Canada and also to Greenland, and these companies must be encouraged to affiliate with existing companies in the Atlantic Provinces in order to develop our fishery resources. Or in the alternative we should attempt to get the Canadian-owned companies to expand, although this may be physically impossible because of their limited number.
This particular piece of legislation is supposed to be of some help to the inshore fishermen, but it has failed in the past. I suppose it represents a nibbling at a very major problem. I am not asking, nor I think are any of us, that we look for a handout here or for something for small inshore fishing operators; but if these people are to increase their productivity they must be given more opportunity than they have had in the past to get the necessary funds to purchase the required gear. As I have said, this particular piece of legislation has not proved to be the answer. Perhaps many feel it is a neat little package which can be defended in certain quarters; but unless and until the proposed changes which the Minister suggested in his opening remarks are brought about, many of us will be unhappy with the situation.
Another important thing is that it is necessary to stress, when talking of fishing, the realization that our future lies in the development of our offshore fisheries, which will require bigger ships and modem and efficient plants. Once again this will require more imagination than has been exhibited by successive governments in past years when talking about development of this particular resource.
There is some consolation in the fact that over the past two years a considerable amount has been done in this regard. But just because problems have been attended to is no reason to ignore other problems which have gone unattended to for a long time. Right now across this country there is a greater awareness than ever before of a battle or war on poverty. This will require an imaginative approach. It is not merely a question of coming up with something somewhere which you think you can defend and then sitting on it for five years or so, saying that you have 22620-168
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act done something about it and that it is not your fault that the fishermen did not take advantage of it. Your attitude should be that if a problem is existing you must find its solution. It is ludicrous and a mockery just to present certain pieces of legislation and then rest upon them, to say that that is what you tried to do, and it is too bad it did not work. Our job is to find something that will work.
In the suggested 14 point program announced a few months ago by the Minister I think he showed this kind of leadership which in coming years will lead to a substantial improvement in incomes of fishermen in Newfoundland, and I congratulate him. But I also know that his task will not be an easy one because there will be those who perhaps will not understand the problems as well as he does. There will also be those who will be pushing him perhaps a little harder than they should, or sometimes a little unrealistically. A combination of those two things is, in my opinion, the best hope for a solution.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few brief remarks about the resolution under consideration. Even though I am taking part in the debate, I am not to be considered as an expert on fisheries, but rather as an amateur who, like the hon.
June 18. 1965

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin), goes trout fishing occasionally. As a matter of fact, I would hope officials of the Department of Fisheries could lend both of us a hand so that we might be luckier and, thus, happier.
A few weeks ago I visited a part of the country where fishing is one of the principal means of subsistence. The fishermen X met there made me promise to take the first opportunity I would have in the house to make their views known to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud).
As you are aware, Mr. Chairman, those fishermen are good citizens and they often experience great hardship in plying their trade. Since the Minister of Fisheries knows very well the conditions under which our fishermen live, he will undoubtedly give all his attention to the problems I will submit to him as briefly as possible.
The New Brunswick fishermen I met asked me to make representations to the minister and ask him to fulfil the promise made to them during the last election campaign, to set up a 12-mile zone. They also asked that it be done as soon as possible.
They also convinced me that a great number of fishermen from other countries still come to our shores in order to benefit from our natural resources which, they feel, belong to them.
These fishermen also reminded me that they had been promised, with much fanfare, that as soon as a Liberal government came to power, their problems would be settled, along with those of all other sectors of the Canadian economy.
But they wonder when the government will take action, because however commendable it may be to lend the fishermen more money, what good is it to open the national coffers so that they may go deeper into debt, if they are not allowed to have a territory in which to earn a decent living?
Mr. Chairman, I shall say no more, except to urge the Minister to act and to put into effect, after two years, what he and his associates of the Maritimes have promised, with so much publicity, during the last electoral campaigns.
The time to act has come and, on behalf of New Brunswick fishermen, I ask the minister to deal with their problems, which he fervently promised to do when he was in opposition.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to hold up the passage of this resolution for any length of time, as I understand it is the intention of the House to complete the consideration of both the resolution and the bill today. I should like to mention one or two points, in view of the fact that there are many fishermen in my constituency who will be affected in a very helpful way by the recommendations contained in this resolution.
Obviously this resolution has been designed to make the fishermen aware of what is available to them in the form of credit. The former Minister of Fisheries pointed out that one third of the loans that had been approved under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, involving 25 per cent of the total amount that has been loaned, have been made to fishermen in the Province of Prince Edward Island. That certainly is not the largest province with a fishing industry, nor does it have the biggest fishing fleet in Canada, and the former Minister of Fisheries can take a good deal of credit in this regard. The people of the Atlantic provinces were much impressed by his policies in respect of this industry when he held the ministerial portfolio. I have no axe to grind with the present Minister of Fisheries, but I should like to say that it would indeed be difficult to find a man more interested in the problems of fishermen and the fisheries industry than the senior Member for Queens, the former Minister of Fisheries.
One of the problems I have encountered in speaking with the fishermen of my constituency relates to the fact that many of them are not anxious to go to banks to obtain loans. Over the years some of them have no doubt encountered difficulty in convincing bank managers that their operations are all that they feel they are. I hope the Minister will make certain that all fishermen are aware of the changes that are to be made to the Act and that the Government will guarantee the loans in question. I hope the
June 18. 1965	COMMONS
Minister can convince these fishermen that they should go to their banks to obtain the loans they require.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
It might well be that we would be better off if we were to establish a board rather than requiring fishermen to go to banks to secure loans. Quite often fishermen and other people are more willing to make application to a Government board for a loan than they are to approach a bank manager for the same purpose. While I do not necessarily know that this would be the solution to the problem, it is quite evident that there is a problem because the fishermen are not taking advantage of the provisions of the Act in the manner we would like them to. There is not much sense in increasing the amount available to fishermen by way of loans if they are not going to go to the banks to borrow the money.
The Minister of Fisheries represents a riding in the Maritime Provinces as I do and he is aware that a great many of our fishermen, especially lobster fishermen, would rather borrow money from the buyers of their product and operate in that manner than go to a bank to secure a loan. If they could be convinced that they could secure loans from the banks by making application for them, certainly they would have a much greater degree of independence than they have now in obtaining loans from the buyers of their product. Quite probably they would also secure a better price for their product and thus be in a much better financial position at the end of the year.
Something has to be done by the Minister and the Department to make fishermen aware of the availability of these loans and of the fact that they can go to a bank and get the money. In my view action must be taken with regard to these two points. As I have said, we might be wiser to set up a board to which fishermen could apply directly for loans, rather than following the present method. There is no doubt there is much more speed and efficiency associated with the securing of a loan under the present method. I am not one who usually wants to promote Government bureaucracy and red tape, but at the same time there is not much sense in having legislation on the statute books if people are not going to take advantage of it.

Mr. Chairman, I believe some hon. Members are expecting replies to the questions they have asked. First, I want to express my appreciation for the support which all Members who have spoken have given to the proposed amendments. I agree with the two hon. Members for Queens and the hon. Member for Cumberland that every possible action should be taken in order to advertise this legislation and try to make it more popular, more practical and, if at all possible, more available to the fishermen. I hope I will not have to agree to the suggestion made by the last Member who spoke, and have my picture put in the newspaper. I believe this would be of no assistance in making the legislation more available to fishermen. I know that most fishermen know me well enough that they do not need to see my picture in the newspapers.
The hon. Member for Comox-Alberni referred to the fishing zone legislation passed some 11 months ago. I have no doubt that the hon. Member is very conscious of his responsibility toward the fishing industry of his province and also of his responsibility in regard to our international relations with other countries. I am sure the hon. Member would not suggest that we take immediate, drastic action that could jeopardize our good international relations by adopting measures which could be detrimental to the fishing industry of his province as well as that of other parts of the country. He suggested in his remarks that nothing has been done about the fisheries development program such as we undertook to do following the Federal-Provincial Conference held some 15 months ago. [DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I am sure that the hon. Member is well aware of the increased assistance which has been granted for the construction of fishing vessels, including vessels built for ground fishing operations in his own Province of British Columbia. I am sure the hon. Member would not suggest we take action now
[Mr. Macquarrie.l
to facilitate the construction of additional fishing vessels for the salmon industry. We would not be logical. According to the statistics advanced by the hon. Member we should exercise some control in an industry which, many of us believe and perhaps rightly, is being over-exploited. We would not be logical, therefore to assist in building more fishing vessels for that particular industry. I could say the same thing about the lobster industry on the Atlantic cost. I do not believe it would be logical for us to provide facilities for the construction of additional lobster fishing boats when we are trying to control this fishery which many of us believe is over-exploited.
The hon. Member knows also of the changes which have been made in the fishermen indemnity plan and the large number of cost-sharing programs which are now under way in the different provinces, along with the centralization program which has been introduced in Newfoundland, as well as the grants assistance program which has been announced by the Prime Minister on June 7 and which would provide in designated areas a subsidy of 33 J per cent for new processing industries or the extension of existing industries. These are only some of the measures which have been introduced recently in order to get this national program under way.
Now, most Members of this House are familiar with the operations of the different provincial loan boards. I do not believe it is the responsibility of the Federal Government to induce or force the Province of British Columbia to establish a provincial loan board. These loan boards have been very effective in the Atlantic Provinces and in the Province of Quebec. They have provided direct lending to fishermen. I am personally familiar with many of them and I had the responsibility of initiating such a board in the Province of New Brunswick in 1946. I was the secretary of that board for over six years. Since then, this board has lent millions of dollars to fishermen in the Province of New Brunswick. Similar boards exist in the Province of Nova Scotia, and other Atlantic Provinces and they have been very successful.
The hon. Member for Cumberland suggested that a Federal loan board might be established. I would be afraid that if such a measure were introduced it would lead to overlapping. Provincial loan boards are more familiar with the needs of the fishermen in

their respective provinces and, as I have said, they have been very effective. I want to say too, that as suggested by the hon. Member for Medicine Hat, we will try to find ways and means for making this legislation better known and, if at all possible, influence the banks to allow the fishermen to take greater advantage of it. The hon. Member for Queens-Lunenburg referred to a pamphlet which has been published to advertise this legislation. Personally, I thought this pamphlet, which was introduced under the previous administration, was quite effective. In view of the suggestion made by the hon. Member, we will try to improve it and make it still better.

The hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Plourde) mentioned, concerning the sale of fish, that the Haitian government made an offer to purchase $3 million worth of fish.
In the fishing industry the difficulty is not to sell fish but to produce an abundance of high quality fish. We can now market all the fish we can produce.
If the province of Quebec, at the time this offer was made, could not meet the requirements as far as quality of quantity is concerned, it is because it was able to sell its catches on markets offering a better price. In the abovementioned case, of which I was aware, the offer related to the purchase of a certain quantity of dried cod for which the market is rather limited. Fishermen of the province of Quebec, like those of the Atlantic provinces, prefer perhaps a more modern or practical way of preparing fish according to the market demand.
As to the remarks of the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard), the government of his province and not the federal government is responsible for trout production.

The hon. Member for Burin-Burgeo has suggested that we should provide credit for fishermen on the same terms as that available for farmers. I must say, Mr. Chairman, that the credit facilities made available to fishermen are comparable to those made available to farmers. I would say in many ways they are superior because we offer to fishermen certain subsidies for the construction of vessels or equipment which are not available to farmers. We provide subsidies of 25 to 50 per cent for the construction of certain types of vessels and there are many farmers who
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act would like to have the same advantage in the purchase of their equipment.
The hon. Member for Queens-Lunenburg referred to the definition of "fisherman". I believe if he had read clauses 2 and 3 of the regulations, he would have noticed that a fisherman was not only a person who had an equitable or legal interest in a fishing vessel but also in a weir or similar fish catching device. If he has any interest in this fishing equipment or if he is qualified for a licence, then he can qualify for a loan.

Perhaps while we are in committee on the resolution I might be permitted to address one or two questions to the Minister which might serve to avoid carrying on an extended discussion at other stages of the bill. I was interested in what the Minister had to say about the credit facilities offered by provincial loan boards in the Atlantic Provinces. He suggested that the funds made available ran into millions of dollars. I can understand that the Minister may not have detailed figures available to him today when we are dealing with Federal legislation, but I should be glad to have further particulars about these loan boards.
I should like to relate this information to remarks I made when I was quoting from a brief by the Government of Newfoundland. The Premier of that Province suggested that loans made to farmers under comparable legislation had been on a scale a thousand times greater than loans to fishermen under fisheries legislation. In order to put this into perspective I should like to refer to a table with which I am sure the Minister is familiar. This table indicates that the net product value of agriculture is some 20 times as great as the net product value of the fisheries. I am trying to get a picture of the total credit facilities available to fishermen as compared with those available to farmers, and the degree to which money available from provincial loan boards closes the gap between 20 to 1 and 1,000 to 1.

speechtext: I do not have complete information with me this afternoon, but the Province of New Brunswick has lent close to $10 million since the inception of their Loan Board Act in 1946. This year I believe more than $2 million was included for this purpose in their estimates. The figures for Nova Scotia may be somewhat higher. In proportion to the number of fishermen in the two provinces, the figures for Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island would be about the same.

I have one other point to raise with reference to the Minister's comment that he was sure I would not want to see more boats and gear go into an already overcrowded salmon industry in British Columbia. Let me make it clear I am one of those who have pointed out that something needs to be done about this situation. On the other hand I have heard many Members of this House representing farming constituencies express concern about what they refer to as vertical integration. My feeling is that vertical integration came to the fishing industry long before the farmers began to talk about it. I am wondering whether or not provision for credit is such as will enable fishermen to extricate themselves from the position in which many of them now find themselves.
Let me make my meaning clear. One of the papers which provides background information for the fisheries conference points out that traditionally many of the borrowing requirements of fishermen have been supplied by the merchants or processors who buy the fish. This source of credit has always been used, though the tendency now is to turn to other sources of credit. I should like the Minister to tell us how far this legislation will go to closing this gap. Are the arrangements adequate to enable a practising fisherman to extricate himself from a state of virtual peonage such as has existed over many years?

There is no doubt this legislation will constitute an improvement compared with the existing legislation. I would point out particularly that the "ceiling" has been raised from $4,000 to $10,000.
Again, I cannot take responsibility for the provisions made by British Columbia which has not its own loan board. Possibly they do not see any need for a further extension of credit. Possibly they consider that over-fishing is already taking place in some cases, and they do not wish to see fishermen engaged in the salmon fishing operation. We are now providing a 50 per cent subsidy on the construction of fishing vessels for groundfish operations on the West Coast. This will be of some assistance. I know that in the Atlantic Provinces fishermen are taking the best possible advantage of the existing loan boards.

subtopic: MR. WINCH-DORION INQUIRY-PRESS REPORT OF FINDINGS
speechtext:
I would like very much, Sir, to raise a matter of not only personal privilege, but I think House of Commons privilege. It is not my intention to quote to Your Honour Standing Orders, custom or precedent. I approach you, Mr. Speaker, on the basis of one point alone, and that is that in your position and under your office and oath you are, Sir, the embodiment of the protection of the rights and privileges of Members of the House of Commons.
My question of privilege, therefore, Sir, on that basis and that basis alone, is to ask your consideration of what in my experience in the 12 years I have been in the House of Commons is one of the greatest insults given to yourself as Speaker, Sir, the Government and the House of Commons, in that in a newspaper published in Ottawa this afternoon, the Ottawa Citizen, there is a report of a Royal Commission, the Dorion Commission. The evidence, Sir, is there for all to see, because in the first paragraph it says:
Chief Justice Frederic Dorion's report on his judicial Inquiry will be handed to the Government on Monday, June 28, the day Prime Minister Pearson returns to his desk from London.
Mr. Speaker, that is ten days from today. Then four paragraphs later it says:
Although inquiry staff will not discuss Judge Dorion's findings, a source who claims to be informed-and whose record in situations of this sort in the past has been remarkably accurate-gives this preview of Judge Dorion's conclusions:
Not only do we then have what purports to be, on this authoritative source, the report of Chief Justice Frederic Dorion but we also have, Sir-and this is of the utmost importance-a photograph on the front page of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Favreau) bearing the caption "Questions", and the picture of another Minister with the caption "Cleared". Then on page 3 the article is headed "Dorion preview". I say, Sir, that this is an absolute insult to the Commissioner, Chief Justice Dorion, an insult to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), an insult to the Government, an insult to the House of Commons, and should be investigated immediately.

I had at the time very serious doubts as to whether there was a real question of privilege, and I would like to refer the hon. Member to Beauchesne's Fourth Edition, Citation 105(2), which says:
It Is the practice in the House of Commons to bring up a question of privilege after prayers, and before the House has taken up the Orders of the Day. Only in very aggravated cases, requiring the immediate interposition of the House, will any business be suddenly interrupted.
The complaint of the hon. Member may or may not be well founded. But I would suggest to him that if there is a question of privilege, which I doubt, but about which I do not feel at this time I should be called upon to make a ruling, this matter should be raised at the proper time. That would be Monday, before the orders of the day.

Briefly, the bill provides for the appointment of two additional Vice Presidents of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Corporation or agency charged with the administration of the National Housing Act. The work of the Corporation over the 20 years
June 18, 1965

that it has been in existence has expanded to such an extent that the appointment of these two additional officers, both in the opinion of the directors of the Corporation and in my opinion as the responsible Minister, is overdue and I hope that this Committee will give speedy consideration to the legislation which permit the appointment of these two additional Vice Presidents.

speakeroldname: Mr. William Dean Howe (Hamilton South) moved
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION TO MENTALLY RETARDED PERSONS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-7, to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act (application to mentally retarded).



June 18. 1965
Juvenile Delinquents Act
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the bill which I have introduced is to confer upon the mentally retarded the protection of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. The philosophy of that Act is now expressed in section 3, subsection 2, which states:
Where a child is adjudged to have committed a delinquency he shall be dealt with, not as an offender, but as one in a condition of deliquency and therefore requiring help and guidance and proper supervision.
This is more fully expressed in section 38 which reads as follows:
This Act shall be liberally construed to the end that its purpose may be carried out, namely, that the care and custody and discipline of a juvenile delinquent shall approximate as nearly as may be that which should be given by its parents, and that as far as practicable every juvenile delinquent shall be treated, not as a criminal, but as a misdirected and misguided child, and one needing aid, encouragement, help and assistance.
In section 2, subsection 1, "child" is defined as meaning "any boy or girl apparently or actually under the age of 16 years, or such other age as may be directed in any province pursuant to subsection 2". The operative word here is "apparently". Our legal processes rest upon the comprehension of the accused of the nature of his crime and of the court proceedings subsequent to it. Chronological age is of no consequence if an accused is mentally defective and unable to comprehend. Therefore in my amendment chronological age and mental age are taken into account in the definition of the word "child".
Section 12 of the Criminal Code states:
No person shall be convicted of an offence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he was under the age of seven years.
Section 13 provides as follows:
No person shall be convicted of an offence in respect of an act or omission on his part while he was seven years of age or more, but under the age of fourteen years, unless he was competent to know the nature and consequences of his conduct and to appreciate that it was wrong.
While mental retardates within these mental age limits cannot be regarded exactly as children of these chronological ages, it is still true that their comprehension is not such that they should be treated as adult criminals. It is within the philosophy of the Juvenile Delinquents Act to accord them the privileges of that Act. They should not, for their own good as well as for the good of the community, be exposed to the usual public and trial processes of the criminal courts. Even if they are adjudged offenders, they can neither comprehend nor benefit from the kind of punishment usually given an adult offender.

Under the Canadian law at present an insane or mentally defective offender may be detained in a place of safekeeping under an order of the Lieutenant Governor of a province and never be brought to trial. This is contained in section 527 of the Criminal Code. I do not believe that such a situation should be allowed to exist, but that is not the point at issue today. The point is that a mentally retarded person can be arrested and charged and be subjected to full publicity. He can be incarcerated for years or for a lifetime with no trial, and he and his family continue to bear the stigma of an unproven crime. This is not permitted to occur in juvenile offences and it should not occur in offences by retardates.
All of us are aware of cases in which the present laws inflict grave hardship. A recent case in Canada involved a man of 25 charged with a criminal offence. His mental age was six years. It was obvious that he did not understand the nature of the crime and certainly did not understand the criminal proceedings brought against him. In addition, he was not even capable of committing the crime. Even so, this case received full publicity at the time, with its attendant hardships upon the family of the accused.
I should like to refer to a statement by Mr. Justice Thompson of the Ontario Supreme Court in which he said that everyone charged with a crime must, as a matter of constitutional right, be capable of understanding the nature of the proceedings and comprehending their course, must be able to plead and properly instruct counsel and be able to make proper and full answer and defence. Children cannot do this. Neither can mental retardates. They should not be charged and prosecuted publicly any more than children should. They are not insane adults; they are retarded adults and they should be given the same legal protection as children. They should enjoy the legal privileges conferred under the Juvenile Delinquents Act, and I urge all hon. Members to give this matter their serious consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING APPLICATION TO MENTALLY RETARDED PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate on Bill No. C-7 having to do with mentally retarded persons and the application to them of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. The bill introduced by the hon. Member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe) proposes to include mentally retarded persons who have a mental age of under 16
June 18. 1965
years or under 18 years according to the discretion of the Governor in Council. The bill also proposes to extend the Act to include the concept of mental age in addition to the factor of chronological age.
In this matter, as in all other matters which involve the social and medical sciences, I think we should take into consideration the whole problem in the light of its historical and present development. The mentally retarded do present difficulties not only in our society endeavouring to obtain social justice for all but, in particular, when trying to apply the laws relating to criminal procedures and rehabilitation practices. While available statistics place the prevalence of clearly established retardation at 3 per cent of the population, a school age population survey showed that there were as high as 10 per cent who if not clinically mentally deficient are at least on the borderline and require special training in school. May I bring to the attention of the hon. Member a statement made by Dr. Henry Dunn, Professor of Pediatrics in the University of British Columbia, who said that this gigantic problem, numerically as well as socially, is the most important chronic disability of children in Canada today.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
So far as our country is concerned, 3 per cent is the generally accepted estimate of those who are mentally retarded-that is persons who have an I.Q. or intelligence quotient below 75. This would mean that there are in Canada approximately 570,000 mentally retarded persons. This also presents us with the problem of a possible annual increase of 14,000. Statistically, these mentally retarded persons can be divided into three groups. First, there are the mildly retarded, those with intelligence quotients of 50 to 75, who are placed in the educatable class. Second, there are the mildly retarded, those with I.Q.'s of 29 to 49 who are considered trainable; and third, the severely retarded, those with I.Q.'s of 0 to 24 who are so severely handicapped that they usually spend the major part of their lives in institutions.
It is true that there are slightly different classifications of the mentally retarded, such as the ones set up by the World Health Organization, according to international statistical classifications and standards. Such minor discrepancies, however, and the dif-
Juvenile Delinquents Act
Now, I draw to the attention of the hon. Member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe) that his statement to the effect that science and technology enable us to define the mental age of a person in terms of equivalent chronological age, is rather an over-simplification. I could quote many references which would indicate, first, that mental retardation is not a singular medical or mental entity but is a multi-faceted phenomenon with many presumptive causes and a wide variety of manifestations. Second, the adequate classification of children or adults as mentally retarded persons cannot be simply accomplished by the routine application of standardized intelligence tests, but entails numerous other assessments and evaluations of a social, medical and psychological kind. Third, that notwithstanding the technical validity of measuring intelligence in terms of mental age, the assumption that an adult is like or can be treated like a child of comparable intelligence is, on various physiological and psychological grounds, untenable.
May I quote from Dr. Dunner Dybwad, Director Mental Retardation Project, International Union for Child Welfare, Geneva, Switzerland. He stated recently that as one reads about and sees in various countries the tremendous advances being made in the social and vocational habilitation of the adolescent and adult retardates, one notes the extent to which objective social conditions produce in some of these individuals problems which are clearly within the field of adult psychiatry, but for which most adult clinics are as yet not prepared to offer supporting and therapeutic services. He continued by saying that the great social and educational advances in mental retardation made during the past ten years in North America, in Europe, Australia and Japan, might well be summarized in the statement that we have conclusively disproven the old myth that the mentally retarded are "eternal children". As countries throughout the world are now mobilizing a major interdisciplinary and interagency attack on mental retardation, the contribution of psychiatry, along with pediatrics and other medical specialties and those of education, rehabilitation and social work, must be increasingly clarified and translated into functioning programs.

Juvenile Delinquents Act habilitation depends a great deal upon guidance and efforts of mental health specialists as well as psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers and also on the joint efforts of educators and criminologists. Assistance to the parental homes, foster homes and the special programs in the reform institutions are included in such efforts. The basic assumption in this field is that the delinquent individuals are amenable to rehabilitation and all such efforts would eventually repay the community for the expenditure of money and professional resources. The mentally ill and mentally defective individuals usually require specialized care different from the typical management of juvenile delinquents. Mentally ill children and adolescents are cared for by psychiatric services on the outpatient basis or in a special institution. Similar programs are developing in Canada in highly specialized care of the mentally defective such as, for instance, at the London, Ontario, Institute for Studies in Mental Deficiencies. Mixing together the three groups of juvenile delinquents, namely mentally ill children, adolescents, and mentally defectives would obviously impair efficient functioning of any of such programs.
Other critics rightly charge that intelligence tests leave untouched many important aspects of personality like interests, motives, attitudes, or social adaptability. One must, however, recall that these tests do not pretend to measure personality. In fact, no one test ever has been devised, and perhaps never will be devised, that measures all aspects of personality. The best procedure, when a complete personality picture is desired, is to make a case study of an individual's background and experience, and to supplement it with a variety of tests, not only those measuring intelligence but also those measuring special aptitudes, achievements, interests, attitudes and other phases of personality.
Many persons were shocked when Terman announced that the average adult intelligence is equal to that of a 16 years old. Even more shocking was the fact that Army Alpha tests placed the level at 14 years. People forget that psychologists define intelligence as capacity to learn, adaptability and mental alertness. In the tests, knowledge, information and experience are kept at a minimum, though these factors are bound to affect performance.
Fortunately, the I.Q. fad which raged during the 1920's and saw the term applied indiscriminately has declined. Intelligence tests
[Mr. Haidasz.l
DEBATES	June 18, 1965
are seen today in wiser perspective. What they can tell and what they cannot tell about a person's capacities are well recognized. They do one thing, that is, indicate mental alertness and learning ability. They do not take into account personality, special aptitudes and achievements, social adjustments, or many other factors that make for success or failure in life.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Therefore, it is open to question whether the presently applied technique of measuring mental deficiency by comparing the development of the defectives to normal development of an average child, is a precise scientific procedure. In simple terms, we recognize the steps of gradual development of intelligence of a so-called average child and compare to such a scale the intelligence displayed by mentally defectives in the so-called intelligence tests. Such an achieved level we call therefore mental age. By that token, while the average child with the chronological age of 12 is expected to pass the intelligence tests for the mental age of 12, a defective individual may reach the same mental age level in the tests while his chronological age may be 14, 16 or 20, depending on the degree of his deficiency. The expression of intelligence in terms of intelligence quotient, or I.Q., is obtained simply by dividing mental age by chronological age, and multiplied by 100 for convenience. The use of I.Q. is a convenient way for comparing various degrees of mental deficiency. At the same time, Dr. Victor Szyrynski, Professor of Psychiatry at the University of Ottawa, reminds us that the amount of intelligence as measured by the intelligence tests remains basically unchanged throughout the lifetime of an individual. We may see practically that when for instance an individual demonstrates at the chronological age of 16 the mental age of 11, this mental age would remain more or less constant for the remaining years of his life, and when he is 30, 40 or 60, his mental age will still be that of an 11 year old individual. Should such an individual benefit indefinitely from provisions of Bill C-7? I see no logical reason for treating a 40, 60 or 80 year old individual accused of criminal offence in juvenile court because his mental age is below 16.
The paradox of this logic becomes even more obvious if we consider children with superior intelligence. Would a 12 year old child with an I.Q. of 150, which gives him a mental age of 18, be considered outside the jurisdiction of a juvenile court?
June 18. 1965

Although the above-described method of measuring intelligence has been of some practical value, it is well known that intelligence tests have serious limitations. Professor Wechsler, one of the most outstanding American authorities on intelligence measurement says:
Most psychologists are aware of the fact that when an adult of 30 years scores a mental age of 12 and a child of 12 scores a mental age of 12 their intelligence is not identical; yet there does not seem to be any general understanding as to why they are not identical. If what we have said above is correct, the answer is not hard to find. The basic reason a mental age of 12 at 12 years does not mean the same things as mental age of 12 at 30 years is that the measured abilities, and hence the mental age scores, represent different portions of the subjects' respective total intelligence. At age 12, the tests are capable of tapping far more of the individual's capacities than at 30.
In a similar way, Professor Coleman in the recent edition of his book "Abnormal Psychology" published in 1964 states:
There has been much criticism of the practice of making diagnosis and/or commitments on the basis of I.Q. alone. For one thing, it is extremely difficult in many cases to make an accurate assessment of intellectual level. This is particularly true in the case of brain-damaged children. Often these children possess genuine ability but have difficulty in making adequate responses because of spasticity, athetosis, defective hearing or vision or other impairments. Even more important, the criterion of adaptive behavior is not revealed in an I.Q.- particularly in the case of individuals with only mild or moderate retardation. Some people with I.Q.s in the low 50s or 60s can support themselves and get along creditably in the community. This is particularly true of those who have received the advantages of training in state or private schools. Consequently, even when an individual's I.Q. is as low as 50, he may or may not need custodial care, depending on the level of his emotional, vocational, and social adjustments. Certainly, when an individual's I.Q. is in the 60s and he is making an adequate adjustment in the community there seems little point in labelling him as a mental retardate.
The situation becomes even more complex when we remember that intelligence measurement depends very largely on co-operation of the subject. It is also well known to psychiatrists and psychologists that results of intelligence tests under emotional stress are not very reliable. Still more, the proper results depend on the motivation of the subject to do his very best during testing. Though it is practically impossible to fake a higher intelligence than one actually possesses, there is nothing easier than to meet the tests with an indifferent, negativistic or malingering attitude in order to provide onself with the low range of mental deficiency. When an individual in trouble with the law realizes that he could change the aspect of legal pro-
Juvenile Delinquents Act cedures by displaying a dull attitude on testing, there would hardly be any objective way to measure his intelligence without going through his school or clinical files where his intelligence may, or may not, be recorded.
Furthermore, judging intelligence from the general behaviour of the individual and from clinical observations is notoriously subject to gross errors. There are mental defectives with unusually appealing "intelligent" expressions on their faces while not infrequently dull and primitive looking individuals may be endowed with supernormal intellectual brightness.
While in some cases mental deficiency and delinquency appear together, the current views are contrary to linking them in a causative relationship. There is an interesting study in the field, an article by Mr. Shulman in the Journal of Criminal Law and Criminology, 1951. It can be found at page 763-

Mr. Speaker, the hon. Member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe) has brought before the House a problem that is connected with that uneasy no man's land between the profession of law and the profession of medicine. Somebody remarked in the past that what was formerly a co-operative endeavour between the two professions has perhaps in recent years become almost a field of conflict. While the measure the hon. Member has put before the House today is perhaps not the best method of achieving the objective which he has in mind, I do not think anyone can question the soundness of his motives in bringing this particular matter before the House. He has indeed put his finger on an inadequacy in the law, an inadequacy in the sense that the mentally retarded person is not in the same situation medically as others, and even to a layman such as myself he is not in the same situation as those who are commonly treated as mentally incompetents under the Criminal Code. I think the changing attitude of our society and many other societies toward people of retarded mentality may in large measure be due to the very earnest efforts of retarded children's organizations over the past ten or more years, which have done their best to bring about in our society a better understanding of the problem of mental retardation. The efforts of these particular groups are not by any means spent, nor have they ceased to be necessary. They have at least achieved a certain success down the road to the ultimate objective whereby the person of mental retardation, and more particularly the mentally retarded child, will no longer be the object of derision, shame or even in some cases, fear, in our society. They have brought to society a recognition of the problem of mental retardation. They have brought this problem into the daylight and have created a concern generally that it should be recognized and dealt with out in the open. By way of aside, perhaps, I may say that no other family and no other group of individuals can take greater credit

for this than the Kennedy family, whose interest in the problem arose from their own experience.
The difficulties of a person with retarded mental faculties are probably no more acute than when he is faced with the law of the land, and more particularly the criminal law; for the law has created a set of standards and procedures which it is assumed an adult person of average intelligence can comprehend in substance and can govern himself accordingly; that is, can comprehend in substance if not in technical detail. However, in the case of a person with retarded mentality, that assumption cannot be made. Problems of procedure, of treatment of the crime, of custody and of ultimate responsibility arise; problems which I may say are analogous to but are not identical with those which arise in dealing with children before the courts. I say they are analogous but not identical, Mr. Speaker, because the fully-grown, chronologically aged person is obviously different from a person of tender years, as has been so well pointed out by my hon. friend and colleague the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Haidasz).
The Juvenile Delinquents Act, which is the measure the hon. Member proposes to amend, was conceived entirely in the context of those of tender years. As the Parliamentary Secretary has already pointed out, it has created a series of measures and a regime of law which, while appropriate to younger persons is, in my submission, inappropriate to the problems, of adults of retarded mentality. I think perhaps the best way to illustrate the problems which I see arising from the shortcomings of the proposed measure would be to make reference to the actual terms of the Act. First there is the question of definitions. Section 2(l)(a) says:
"child" means any boy or girl apparently or actually under the age of 16 years, or such other age as may be directed in any province pursuant to subsection (2);
Subsection (2) of the same section authorizes the Governor in Council by proclamation to-
-direct that in any province the expression "child" in this Act means any boy or girl apparently or actually under the age of 18 years-
In fact in five provinces in Canada the age for the purposes of this Statute is as follows: In Saskatchewan, Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island the age has been established to be 16. In the Provinces of British Columbia, Manitoba and Quebec a proclamation has been made under
June 18, 1965	COMMONS
the Statute establishing the age limit at 18. In the Province of Alberta the age limit has been established at the level of 18 for girls and 16 for boys. In the Province of Newfoundland the provincial laws, so I am advised, under the Terms of Union still continue to govern the situation and have set the age at 17, the Juvenile Delinquents Act not having been proclaimed in respect of that Province.
The Statute, therefore, is very obviously intended for those of tender years. I would agree with the hon. Member for Parkdale who has pointed out that, for example, the intelligence test used to determine the mental age of children can be very deceptive and is obviously dependant upon a great many complicated factors. The choice of a chronological age is no more accurate or scientific than the choice of age by means of an intelligence test, but the choice of the chronological age does indicate the difficulties which legislatures have had in the past in providing a criterion and a dividing point which those responsible for the administration of the law may readily apply with some certainty of administering justice. Section 4 of the Statute provides:
Save as provided in section 9. the Juvenile Court has exclusive jurisdiction in cases of delinquency Including cases where, after the committing of the delinquency, the child has passed the age limit-
-to which I have already referred. This means that the ordinary courts of the land, depending upon the nature of the offence-the Magistrate's Court, the County Court, for example, in the Province of Ontario, or the High Court of Justice-do not have the jurisdiction at all over someone fitting within the criteria of the Statute. That jurisdiction has been removed altogether and has been put into the Juvenile Courts. The effect of these provisions and the difficulty of their application may be further illustrated by referring to section 8(1) which provides as follows:
When any child is arrested, with or without a warrant, such child shall, instead of being taken before a justice, be taken before the Juvenile Court: and, if a child is taken before a justice, upon a summons or under a warrant or for any other reason, it is the duty of the justice to transfer the case to the Juvenile Court, and of the officer having the child in charge to take the child before that Court, and in any such case the Juvenile Court shall hear and dispose of the case in the same manner as if such child had been brought before it upon information originally laid therein.
What is clear, therefore, is that there is an absolute obligation on the police and the prosecuting authorities to determine the age of the child with reference to this particular
DEBATES	2655
Juvenile Delinquents Act Statute, and when the determination is made in the particular Province, whether it be 16, 17 or 18, if the child is below that age there is an obligation upon the authorities to bring the child before the Juvenile Court. As a matter of law, any proceedings taken in the ordinary criminal courts in relation to such child would therefore be null and void.
Therefore there is an obvious importance initially in the fact that the police and the prosecuting authorities should be able to make the determination as to whether or not a child comes within the Statute.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
There is also an obvious initial difficulty for an arresting officer in the case proposed by the hon. Member for Hamilton South (Mr. Howe), for what he is requiring the policeman or Crown Prosecutor to do is to make a determination as a layman of a very difficult technical question, a question on which in the case of a particular issue qualified medical practitioners may differ.
As the Parliamentary Secretary has already pointed out, there is no final and obvious criterion for deciding this question of mental age. He also pointed out that he would take issue with the suggestion made in the explanatory note that this is readily determinable. If there is difficulty in determining this question for qualified medical practitioners, then I suggest the difficulty is even greater when the initial determination is made by an arresting officer. Therefore the bill places on the police and the prosecuting authorities the obligation of making a scientific judgment.
The difficulty of such a judgment in relation to matters of law is illustrated, I think, by a passage I would like to refer the House to in a monograph called "Psychiatry and the Law", by Manfred S. Guttmacher, Chief Medical Officer of the Supreme Bench of Baltimore, and Henry Weihofen, Professor of Law at the University of New Mexico. I refer to chapter 8 of this book which deals with congenital intellectual deficiency, which is the definition with which the learned authors choose to describe the situation which I believe the hon. Member has in mind. At page 171 they say:
The fact that we have instruments for the measurement of intelligence has created the false impression that we now know what it is we are measuring and that we can measure it exactly. Even some workers in the psychological sciences fall into this error. The medical author some years ago observed an extreme example of this when he was guest lecturer in a college course on abnormal psychology. The professor in charge of the course advised the students not to be content with the
June 18. 1965

Juvenile Delinquents Act usual method of computing the I.Q., hut to he more exact and make use of decimals 1
It is highly desirable that lawyers and judges have a functional and realistic view of intelligence. In deciding whether a person with defective intelligence has sufficient capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness of his act, it is necessary to take into consideration whether the act is perpetrating a fraud or committing a murder. Doubtless many persons with somewhat defective intelligence are incapable of appreciating some of the intricacies of the law of fraud, and yet are fully aware of the enormity of homicide.
In the same work at page 174 the following is found:
Most of the intellectually defective individuals do not have marked physical abnormalities. Many of them have a wholly normal physical appearance. The people who pride themselves on their ability to judge intelligence and character by appearances had better not put their judgment to objective scientific test or they will be greatly disappointed. But many rely heavily on physical appearance in reaching their conclusions.
From the particular text to which I have referred, Mr. Speaker, and from the remarks made by the hon. Member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz), it is obvious that the kind of criteria which are necessary for the police authorities and the courts to make this initial determination on these questions are just not present in the case of mental age. One of the shortcomings of this particular proposed piece of legislation is that it provides no standard or basis upon which mental age is to be determined. It provides no procedure whereby initially the opinion of qualified medical practitioners is to be taken to determine whether or not the court has jurisdiction and that the proper proceedings have been taken. Indeed, by treating the person of advanced years but of retarded mentality in the same way as juvenile delinquents without providing the appropriate administration to deal with such a person would only risk upsetting the arrangements which have been made, perhaps not altogether satisfactorily but with some success, with regard to juvenile delinquents.
This may be illustrated by making reference to the Statute itself. There is the fact that under the Juvenile Delinquents Act a delinquent is not to be detained in normal circumstances with other adult persons but is to be kept with persons of tender years. In applying the Juvenile Delinquents Act to the case of a person of advanced years but who is mentally retarded, it has already been pointed out that a grown man is not to be treated in the same way as a small child, because he is not the same type of person. Similarly section 23 of the Statute refers to

the responsibilities of the Children's Aid Society and particularly to foster homes into whose custody and under whose control the objects of the Juvenile Delinquents Act are to be kept before and after they attend their trial. I think all hon. Members will agree that it is obviously inappropriate to put under the care of the Children's Aid Society, when dealing with what is a distinct medical problem, the social and practical problem of a grown person who is mentally retarded.
The substance of my objections, therefore, would be that, agreeing as I do with the ultimate objectives of the hon. Member in introducing the measure, agreeing as I do that someone who is shown to be mentally retarded should not be treated in the same way under our law as someone who is entirely mentally defective, I do not feel it is appropriate to treat this type of mentally retarded person under the provisions of the Juvenile Delinquents Act. That statute was, as I have indicated, prepared with a distinct factual situation in mind. It was prepared with organizations such as juvenile institutions, Children's Aid Societies, foster homes and probation officers in mind. It would be altogether inappropriate to add to the provisions of that measure responsibility for dealing with what is an entirely different practical and medical problem, that of the person of advanced years who is mentally retarded.
I believe it is six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.
